Nigeria Payments Report 2025
Victoria Olaonipekun
Published 16th MAY 2025
Nigeria’s payment landscape is transforming rapidly, driven by fintech innovation, regulatory reforms, and evolving consumer preferences. Nigeria’s payment landscape is transforming rapidly, driven by fintech innovation, regulatory reforms, and evolving consumer preferences.
The ecosystem remains resilient despite a 54% drop in African fintech funding in 2023. Nigeria continues to lead in fintech adoption and investment, attracting $140 million in H1 2024 alone and hosting over 200 fintech startups, the highest in Africa. The country also processed ₦1.56 quadrillion in e-payment transactions in just the first half of 2024, representing 70% of the total volume recorded in 2023, underscoring the sector’s sustained growth.
This report, developed by TC Insights in partnership with Zone, provides a comprehensive analysis of Nigeria’s digital payments evolution, covering transaction trends, cross-border payments, emerging technologies, fraud risks, and the regulatory shifts shaping the ecosystem. It also explores future-forward topics like embedded finance and the rollout of open banking frameworks.
The Nigerian Payments Report 2025 offers policymakers, fintechs, investors, and other stakeholders data-driven insights to help understand where the market is today and where it is headed.

Building on the foundation of the previous edition, the 2025 edition delivers deeper insight, sharper data, and a new benchmark: the National Payments Scorecard . With expanded coverage of innovation, regulation, and infrastructure, this report examines how players across fintech, banking, and policy are shaping a faster, smarter, and more secure digital payment future.
Download Report
Nigeria Payments Report 2025 – Summary
Nigeria’s payment landscape has entered a new phase of acceleration driven by the rise of real-time digital infrastructure, growing mobile-first adoption, and the expanding role of regulated innovation.
In just the first half of 2024, internet transfers accounted for over ₦828 trillion in transaction value, underscoring the dominant role of digital rails in everyday financial activity. Mobile apps, embedded finance solutions, and blockchain-based reconciliation are reshaping how value moves, not only faster, but with greater transparency and trust.
The Nigeria Payments Report 2025 , produced by Zone in partnership with TechCabal Insights, builds on the foundation laid by the 2024 edition and goes further. It introduces the National Payments Scorecard , a new benchmark framework for evaluating Nigeria’s payment ecosystem across infrastructure, efficiency, reach, and trust.
The report explores emerging technologies, fraud risks, and cross-border opportunities, while also analyzing consumer behavior, payment channel performance, and the role of regulation in enabling more inclusive, resilient financial systems.
As the second edition in Zone’s annual insight series, the 2025 report provides a deeper, more structured perspective for stakeholders looking to understand the future of payments in Nigeria.

CBN's New Payments Circular: What Banks & Fintechs Must Do Before 2027
Jun 19
Written by Emmanuel Eyo
The Central Bank of Nigeria
1. Introduction
On June 15, 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria issued Circular PSS/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004 , signed by Rakiya O. Yusuf, Director of the Payments System Supervision Department. It is addressed to deposit money banks, microfinance banks, mobile money operators, switching and processing companies, payment terminal and solution service providers, super agents, and all other licensed payment operators.
The circular introduces four simultaneous interventions: payment data localisation , market share caps , ultimate beneficial ownership (UBO) disclosure , and systemic oversight measures . Each carries distinct obligations and deadlines.
The CBN's rationale is that the rapid growth of digital payments has created structural concerns like market concentration among dominant operators, opacity of ownership, and over-reliance on foreign infrastructure. This circular addresses all four at once.
2. Data Localisation
All payment participants in Nigeria must ensure that payment transaction data generated within Nigeria is stored and managed within Nigeria, in line with applicable data protection laws. Full compliance is required by January 1, 2027 .
The scope is wide. Transaction records, BVN data, card data, settlement records, payment instructions, authentication credentials, associated metadata, and the systems that consume this data; fraud models, analytics pipelines, risk-scoring engines are all covered.
Critically, access is itself a form of processing: a foreign-based team with login access to your Nigerian payment data constitutes a cross-border transfer, regardless of where the servers sit.
The obligation attaches to the data, not the company's domicile. Foreign-headquartered platforms processing Nigerian user transactions are squarely within scope.
This directive reinforces the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 , the Central Bank of Nigeria Regulatory Framework for Bank Verification Number Operations , and the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act 2020.
3. Market Structure Requirements
The circular caps market dominance across the two core segments of the card payments chain. Any institution controlling more than 25% of card issuing within a rolling 12-month period cannot simultaneously hold more than 15% of merchant acquiring and vice versa.
To clarify: card issuing is the provision of debit, credit, and prepaid cards to customers. Merchant acquiring is the processing of card payments on behalf of merchants. The CBN's concern is that operators dominating both ends of this chain simultaneously create systemic dependencies and harm competition.
The caps apply at group level, across all affiliated entities. A group routing card issuing through one subsidiary and merchant acquiring through another is not exempt.
All regulated entities must submit monthly market share returns using CBN-prescribed templates. Full compliance is required by December 31, 2026, one day before the data localisation deadline.
4. Ultimate Beneficial Ownership Disclosure
All deposit money banks, PSPs, and other financial institutions with digital payments operations must disclose the Ultimate Beneficial Ownership (UBO) of significant shareholders.
in line with Nigeria's AML/CFT laws. Institutions must maintain accurate, up-to-date UBO records and produce them to the CBN on request.
A beneficial owner is the natural person who ultimately owns or controls a legal entity, even through layers of intermediate companies, trusts, or nominees. The CBN is concerned that complex ownership structures have been used to obscure control of regulated entities, creating risks around money laundering, illicit flows, and regulatory accountability.
The obligation connects to CAMA 2020 register of members requirements and SCUML/NFIU obligations. For institutions with foreign investors, parent companies, or layered holding structures, the practical task is confirming that your shareholder register identifies the natural persons at the top of the chain and is ready to be produced on demand.
This is an ongoing obligation, not a one-time filing. Changes in shareholding that affect beneficial ownership must be updated promptly.
5. Enforcement and Risk
The CBN has stated explicitly that compliance will be monitored and supervisory sanctions imposed where necessary. The recent enforcement actions against fintech platforms confirm that the CBN acts publicly and at scale.
Beyond regulatory sanctions, there is material investor risk: compliance is now a due diligence indicator. A documented failure to implement a CBN circular covering four separate obligations is a governance red flag that affects deal terms and can stall funding rounds.
Where to Begin
Audit your Data Footprint
Commission a structured assessment of every system, vendor, and integration that touches Nigerian payment data. Establish server locations, data types, contracts, and remote access points for each.
Assess your market share
Calculate your card issuing and merchant acquiring share across all affiliated entities over a rolling 12 months. The 25%/15% cap applies to groups, not individual licences.
Trace your ownership chain
Identify your ultimate beneficial owners, update your records, and establish a process for keeping them current and available to the CBN on demand.
Build a staged migration plan
Prioritise by data sensitivity and transaction volume. Start with core payment processing infrastructure and work outward. Build testing windows between each stage.
Review and renegotiate vendor contracts
Identify which providers offer Nigerian data residency and which do not. For those that do not, begin finding alternatives or negotiating bespoke arrangements now.
Run a joint NDPA compliance check
The data localisation obligation overlaps substantially with the NDPA's cross-border transfer rules. A joint programme addressing both frameworks is more efficient and better positioned for regulatory scrutiny.
This publication is a general legal overview and does not constitute legal advice.

The Central Bank of Nigeria’s new payments system circular: What banks, fintechs and investors need to know
Introduction Nigeria’s digital payments ecosystem has experienced remarkable growth over the past decade. In response, the Central Bank of Nigeria
Nkem Umeadi-Onyedika
August 12, 2026
7 min read
Listen to this article
Share
Introduction
Nigeria’s digital payments ecosystem has experienced remarkable growth over the past decade. In response, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) issued its circular titled “Introduction of Market Structure Requirements, Data Localisation, Ultimate Beneficial Ownership Disclosure, and Systemic Oversight Measures in the Nigeria Payments System.” The circular introduces a comprehensive framework to strengthen competition, improve transparency, enhance operational resilience, and safeguard the country’s payment infrastructure.
For banks, fintech companies, payment service providers (PSPs), investors, and corporate groups operating within Nigeria’s payments ecosystem, the circular represents more than just another compliance obligation and raises interpretive and structural questions that will require reassessing business models, ownership structures, technology infrastructure, and expansion plans.
Why the CBN Introduced These Measures
According to CBN, the reforms became necessary following the rapid expansion of electronic payments and digital financial services across the country. The rapid evolution of the digital landscape and increasing digitalisation of financial services have driven the growth of electronic payments, delivering significant benefits including improved efficiency in payment systems. At the same time, there have been several emerging risks such as the increased concentration of market power among a few dominant operators, growing dependence on foreign infrastructure for critical payment data, and limited transparency regarding the true owners of payment institutions.
The circular therefore seeks to ensure that innovation continues, but within a competitive, transparent, and resilient regulatory environment. Two deadlines anchor these reforms: market-structure compliance and data localisation.
December 31, 2026 – Institutions exceeding 25% market share threshold in card issuing or merchant acquiring must achieve the required caps.
January 1, 2027 – All payment transaction data generated in Nigeria must be stored and managed on servers within Nigeria.
Market Structure
One of the most significant aspects of the circular is the introduction of market-structure requirements aimed at preventing excessive concentration in the payments industry. The circular provides that any licensed financial institution that holds more than 25% market share in card issuing within a rolling 12-month period is restricted to a maximum of 15% market share in merchant acquiring over the same period. Conversely, any institution holding more than 25% market share in merchant acquiring may not hold more than 15% market share in card issuing within that same rolling 12-month period.
For context, a merchant acquirer means “a CBN licensed institution that has agreement with the relevant card scheme to contract with merchants to accept payment cards as means of payment.” Card issuing is the business of providing payment instruments, such as cards, to customers for initiating payment transactions. A card issuer is therefore a licensed financial institution that issues these payment tokens or payment instruments to customers. For example, where a bank enables a supermarket to accept Visa or Mastercard payments and processes those transactions on the supermarket’s behalf, the bank is acting as the merchant acquirer, while the bank that issued the customer’s card is the card issuer.
The CBN’s concern is that an operator dominant on one side could leverage that strength to dominate the other. In addition, it requires all regulated entities to submit monthly market share returns to the CBN using prescribed templates and timelines that are, however, yet to be issued.
The practical implications of the circular may necessitate genuine structural change for operators with strong positions across both issuing and acquiring well before the December 2026 deadline. It will include divesting parts of a business, separating activities into distinct legal entities, or voluntarily scaling back in one segment to remain active in another. Each of these options will carry significant corporate, tax, competition, and contractual rearrangements.
Mandatory Data Localisation
Perhaps the most widely discussed aspect of the circular is the mandatory localisation of payment transaction data. Currently, a significant portion of Nigerian payment transaction data is hosted on servers outside the country through international cloud infrastructure. In simple terms, data localisation means that the records of payments made in Nigeria must be stored and managed on servers physically located within Nigeria, in accordance with applicable Nigerian data protection law. The requirement applies broadly across financial institutions and participants facilitating payments in the country, with full compliance expected by January 1, 2027.
The objective behind the requirement is understandable, considering that reports have disclosed that Nigeria is estimated to spend approximately US$850 million annually on offshore data hosting, with nearly 90% of its data hosted outside the country, coupled with the growing importance of payment data as critical national infrastructure and the exponential growth of digital payments. As a result, regulators are increasingly seeking greater data sovereignty and visibility over transactions occurring within their jurisdiction.
A key concern is that the circular is unlikely to affect all institutions equally. Commercial banks typically built their core systems on physical, locally hosted infrastructure long before the widespread adoption of cloud computing. As a result, cloud services are often layered onto existing on-premise environments for specific functions, meaning compliance may largely involve auditing and validating existing data storage arrangements. By contrast, many fintechs and mobile payment service providers were built as cloud-native organisations, with core operations heavily dependent on cloud infrastructure. For these entities, compliance is likely to require more extensive operational and technological changes, including migrating and localising critical payment data and systems.
However, this has a few business implications for companies which currently rely on global cloud platforms or multinational data centres. These institutions may need to migrate payment databases to Nigerian infrastructure, review and renegotiate cloud and outsourcing agreements, update their cybersecurity frameworks, reassess cross-border data-transfer mechanisms, and confirm continued compliance with Nigerian data protection legislation.
Ultimate Beneficial Ownership Disclosure
CBN now requires regulated institutions with digital payment operations to maintain accurate and up-to-date records of their Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBOs) and to make that information available to the regulator on request. An Ultimate Beneficial Owner is the natural person who ultimately owns or exercises effective control over a company, regardless of how many intermediary holding companies or investment vehicles sit in between.
This circular builds upon the CBN’s earlier Guidance on Beneficial Ownership of Legal Persons and Legal Arrangements. This obligation expressly ties into and reinforces existing Anti-Money Laundering, Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Countering Proliferation Financing of Weapons of Mass Destruction in Financial Institutions Regulations, 2022 (AML/CFT).
This will ensure that CBN can access and supervise the payment system during investigations, regulatory examinations, fraud incidents, and enforcement proceedings without relying on infrastructure outside its jurisdiction. For companies with complex corporate governance structures, this requires a careful mapping of the ownership chain down to the natural person, and a considered view on how disclosure interacts with confidentiality obligations to investors.
Practical Compliance Steps for Financial Institutions, FinTech Companies and Payment Service Providers
In response to the CBN circular, these operators within the financial sector should prioritise the following practical compliance actions:
For Market Structure
– Assess consumer issuing and merchant acquiring market shares on a rolling 12‑month basis, including across related entities, to monitor compliance with the 25%/15% market concentration thresholds.
– Implement remediation measures where concentration limits may be exceeded to achieve compliance.
– Submit monthly market share returns to the CBN in the prescribed format and timelines.
For Data Localisation
– Review where payment transaction data is stored, processed, accessed, and backed up to identify any offshore hosting or processing arrangements.
– Update data governance frameworks, policies, and vendor arrangements to ensure ongoing compliance with data localisation requirements.
For UBO Disclosure
– Review ownership structures to identify the natural persons who ultimately own or control significant shareholdings.
– Maintain accurate and up-to-date UBO records, supported by appropriate due diligence and periodic verification processes.
– Establish governance processes to ensure UBO information can be promptly provided to the CBN upon request.
Implications for Investors
The Circular is also expected to have a significant impact on investment activity within Nigeria’s fintech sector. Investors conducting due diligence on financial institutions will need to expand the scope of their reviews beyond traditional financial and commercial considerations. They should assess a target company’s readiness to comply with the new data localisation requirements, the transparency of its ultimate beneficial ownership disclosures, its regulatory reporting obligations, and the strength of its governance and compliance frameworks.
Beyond due diligence, the Circular is likely to influence how transactions are structured and executed. Buyers considering acquisitions or strategic investments should assess at an early stage whether the proposed transaction would trigger any regulatory approval requirements, including obtaining the CBN’s approval for a change in control or whether the combined entity could exceed the prescribed market-share thresholds, which may require the transaction to be restructured before completion.
These regulatory requirements are also likely to affect transaction documentation. For example, parties may include conditions requiring the necessary regulatory approvals to be obtained before closing, while buyers may seek warranties confirming the target’s compliance with the Circular, including its data localisation and disclosure obligations.
Looking Ahead
The Circular reflects a broader shift in the CBN’s regulatory approach towards greater oversight of Nigeria’s payments ecosystem. Its emphasis on data localisation, ownership transparency, market structure, and systemic oversight signals the CBN’s intention to strengthen domestic control over critical payment infrastructure while promoting transparency, competition, and financial stability. For regulated institutions, the implications extend beyond compliance and affect technology and outsourcing arrangements and corporate governance decisions.

CBN payment rules may raise costs, reshape fintech market says PwC
By : Benjamin Alade
Date:
28 October 2026 5:35pm WAT
Share :
Follow Us on Google Discover
CBN Governor, Olayemi Cardoso
CBN Governor, Olayemi Cardoso
The Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) new payment system regulations could increase compliance costs for financial technology companies and other payment service providers, while creating fresh investment opportunities in local data centres, cloud infrastructure and cybersecurity, according to PwC.
In a report titled CBN Data Localisation and Market Structure Rules: Regulatory, Strategic and Technology Implications for Nigeria’s Payment Sector, PwC said the measures would require operators to reassess their business models, technology infrastructure and ownership structures ahead of two compliance deadlines at the end of 2026 and the beginning of 2027.
The CBN issued the circular on June 15, 2026, introducing market structure requirements, mandatory data localisation, ultimate beneficial ownership disclosure and enhanced systemic oversight across Nigeria’s payments ecosystem.
The rules apply to deposit money banks, microfinance banks, mobile money operators, switching and processing companies, payment terminal service providers, payment solution service providers, super agents and other licensed payment operators.
Advertisement
Under the market structure provisions, licensed operators that individually or as part of a group control more than 25 per cent of the market in consumer issuing or merchant acquiring must limit their market share to no more than 15 per cent in the other activity during the same rolling 12-month period.
The CBN also requires affected institutions to submit monthly market share returns in accordance with prescribed templates and timelines.
PwC said the requirements could force some dominant operators to reconsider integrated business models that combine payment instrument issuance, merchant acquisition, processing and other services.
Depending on how market share is measured and further regulatory clarification, affected institutions could consider divesting assets, winding down certain business lines or moderating expansion in one segment.
Advertisement
However, the report stressed that these are possible commercial responses rather than outcomes specifically prescribed by the CBN.
It warned that restructuring could erode business value if companies are forced to dispose of assets within a short period or struggle to find credible buyers. Scaling back operations could also reduce the efficiencies that integrated platforms derive from shared infrastructure, customer relationships and data.
PwC identified the definition of the relevant market as a major implementation challenge, noting that payment activities span card issuance, mobile money, instant transfers, point-of-sale acquiring, QR payments and digital wallets.
It said the regulator and operators would need clarity on whether market share would be calculated by transaction volume, value, transaction count or active users, as well as how group entities, agency networks and white-label arrangements would be treated.
The report added that the market structure rules could redistribute transaction flows across the sector, creating opportunities for smaller banks, fintech companies and independent payment providers to secure new partnerships and merchant relationships.
However, it cautioned that the benefits would depend on whether emerging players could combine regulatory compliance, reliable infrastructure and competitive services.
On data governance, the CBN requires payment transaction data generated in Nigeria to be stored and managed within the country in line with applicable data protection laws, including the Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023.
The deadline for full compliance with the data localisation requirement is January 1, 2027, while operators must meet the market structure requirements by December 31, 2026.
PwC said the localisation rule could place significant financial pressure on smaller fintech companies that rely on international cloud providers for affordable and scalable technology infrastructure.
According to the report, replicating the reliability, security and service standards of global cloud providers locally could require substantial capital investment, potentially favouring larger operators with stronger financial capacity.
Advertisement
It noted, however, that the policy could stimulate demand for Nigerian data centres, local cloud services, cybersecurity capabilities and related technology infrastructure, encouraging domestic and foreign investment.
The report said foreign-backed payment businesses might also deepen their local presence and partnerships to meet the new requirements.
Beyond relocating primary databases, PwC warned that institutions would need to examine the wider movement and management of payment data across backup systems, disaster-recovery facilities, analytics platforms, third-party processors and technology vendors.
It said merely hosting a primary database in Nigeria might not be sufficient to demonstrate compliance if offshore copies of payment transaction data remained in backups, logs, testing environments or third-party systems.
The report also highlighted potential implications for fraud detection, artificial intelligence and analytics platforms that rely on globally distributed data environments.
Financial institutions, it said, would need to determine whether their existing technology arrangements could support localisation without weakening fraud controls, service reliability or business continuity.
PwC recommended that operators map their payment data flows, review hosting arrangements, update vendor contracts and establish technical evidence demonstrating where transaction data is stored, processed, replicated and accessed.
It also urged institutions to assess their ownership structures and beneficial ownership registers to meet disclosure obligations.
Although the CBN circular requires disclosure of the ultimate beneficial owners of significant shareholders, PwC noted that the term was not explicitly defined in the document.
The firm said existing CBN guidance and other regulatory instruments use a five per cent ownership or voting-rights threshold in identifying beneficial ownership interests, suggesting that operators could seek clarification from the regulator on whether this would serve as an appropriate compliance benchmark.
The CBN has indicated that it will monitor compliance and may impose supervisory sanctions under existing laws, regulations and guidelines.
PwC said the compressed implementation schedule would require institutions to undertake market assessments, technology migration, contract renegotiations and possible business restructuring within a short period.
It added that the rules could influence investment decisions in the payments industry, as investors weigh compliance costs and restrictions on scale against opportunities arising from stronger governance and local technology infrastructure.
The firm said the long-term impact would depend on how effectively the regulations balance competition, operational efficiency and systemic resilience.
It warned that restricting the scale of individual operators without strengthening shared payment infrastructure and interoperability could fragment the market and reduce the ability of Nigerian companies to compete with global payment platforms.
Nevertheless, PwC said stronger regulatory oversight, greater ownership transparency and increased investment in local infrastructure could improve confidence among consumers, merchants and investors.
It advised payment operators to begin compliance planning early, seek clarification from the CBN on unresolved technical and market measurement issues, and align their technology investments with the business models they intend to operate after the deadlines.
The report concluded that the rules represent a significant shift in the regulation of Nigeria’s digital payments industry, with compliance likely to require more than administrative adjustments and potentially drive changes in business strategy, infrastructure investment and market competition.

Fintech Licence Requirements in Nigeria (2026): Capital, Fees & CBN Process
Nigeria
· Business Registration
· Published Feb 12, 2026 · Updated Oct 14, 2026
Fintech Licence Requirements in Nigeria (2026): Capital, Fees & CBN Process
Key takeaways
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) licenses fintechs in distinct categories — Switching and Processing, Mobile Money Operator (MMO), Payment Solution Service Provider (PSSP), Payment Terminal Service Provider (PTSP), Super Agent, Payment Service Bank (PSB) and digital Microfinance Bank (MFB) — each under the Banks and Other Financial Institutions Act (BOFIA) 2020.
You must meet two separate financial bars: a minimum paid-up share capital and a distinct, refundable escrow deposit. They are not the same money.
The escrow is returned to you (with any accrued interest) once your final licence is granted or your application is rejected. It is not a fee and it cannot be spent on operations.
Licensing is a two-stage journey: Approval-in-Principle (AIP) first, then the Final Licence after inspection.
Compliance with the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) and Anti-Money Laundering (AML) rules is mandatory, and fintechs that cross the data-processing threshold are treated as Data Controllers of Major Importance.
Read us often? Add Lawzana as a preferred source so our articles surface more in your Google results.
Add to Preferred Sources
In this article
Checklist for Fintech Approval-in-Principle (AIP) in Nigeria
CBN Fintech Licence Classification: PSSP, MMO, Switching, PSB and Digital Banking
Minimum Paid-up Capital and the Separate Escrow Deposit
Compliance with Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Data Privacy
Projected Legal and Regulatory Filing Costs
Nigeria as a Regulatory Path for African Fintech
Common Misconceptions
FAQ
When to Hire a Lawyer
Next Steps
Getting a fintech off the ground in Nigeria comes down to one regulator and a fork in the road: the CBN licenses payment companies in seven main categories, and the one you pick decides everything from your capital bill to what you are legally allowed to touch. Capital requirements run from ₦50 million for a Super Agent to ₦5 billion for a Payment Service Bank or a National MFB — and on top of that sits a separate refundable escrow deposit. Most early-stage startups should start with a PSSP and scale up; the costliest mistakes happen when founders confuse the licence tiers or treat the escrow as a fee. This guide walks through the categories, the real numbers, and the CBN process for 2026.
Checklist for Fintech Approval-in-Principle (AIP) in Nigeria
A timeline showing the 5 stages of obtaining a fintech license in Nigeria.
Before you can launch, you need an Approval-in-Principle. The AIP lets you build your infrastructure and systems, but it does not authorise live commercial transactions — that right only comes with the Final Licence.
Use this checklist to make sure your application package is complete before it reaches the CBN. Incomplete documentation — especially a vague objects clause or a missing policy framework — is the single most common reason applications stall at this stage:
Certificate of Incorporation: Copy of the CAC (Corporate Affairs Commission) certificate for a Nigerian-incorporated company.
Memorandum and Articles of Association (MEMART): Must state clearly that the company's object is to provide the specific fintech service being applied for — a generic objects clause draws a query.
Business Plan: A detailed 3–5 year projection covering financial statements, market analysis, and product roadmap.
Tax Clearance Certificate: Evidence of tax compliance for the company and its directors over the last three years.
Evidence of Escrow Deposit: A bank statement or letter confirming the refundable escrow has been deposited into the designated CBN account.
Fitness and Propriety Questionnaires: Completed forms for all major shareholders, directors, and top management staff.
IT Policy: Detailed documents covering cybersecurity, business continuity, and disaster recovery.
AML/CFT Policy: A comprehensive framework for Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism.
CBN Fintech Licence Classification: PSSP, MMO, Switching, PSB and Digital Banking
Nigeria deliberately silos fintech activities so that risk stays contained and oversight stays specialised. Your licence dictates exactly what you can do — and, just as importantly, what you cannot.
Since the CBN's landmark circular of 9 December 2020, payment companies have been organised into a tiered structure and supervised directly by the CBN as Other Financial Institutions (OFIs) under BOFIA 2020. The main categories are:
Switching and Processing: Facilitates the clearing, settlement, and switching of payment transactions between financial institutions. Powerful, but expensive and tightly restricted.
Mobile Money Operator (MMO): Issues e-money, creates digital wallets, and delivers financial services over mobile phones. Crucially, MMOs may hold customer funds.
Payment Solution Service Provider (PSSP): Operates the "pipes" of the payment system — gateways, merchant portals, and transaction-processing software. It cannot hold customer deposits. Processors of the Paystack/Flutterwave type typically operate in this category, which is why most startups begin here.
Payment Terminal Service Provider (PTSP): Deploys and maintains physical Point-of-Sale (PoS) terminals.
Super Agent: Manages networks of agents for agency-banking services on behalf of licensed institutions.
Payment Service Bank (PSB): A bank-like licence aimed at financial inclusion, able to take deposits and offer payments but barred from lending and foreign-exchange trading.
Digital Banking (Microfinance Bank): To lend and take deposits through a digital-only interface, you need a Tier-1, Tier-2, State, or National MFB licence.

Minimum Paid-up Capital and the Separate Escrow Deposit
Bar chart comparing capital requirements for different Nigerian fintech licenses.
Here is the distinction that trips up the most founders: paid-up share capital and the CBN escrow deposit are two different sums of money. The paid-up capital is the shareholders' funds that capitalise your company and stay in the business. The escrow is a separate amount you lodge with the CBN to demonstrate commitment while your application is reviewed.
That deposit is not a fee. It comes back. Once your Final Licence is issued — or your application is rejected — the escrow is refunded to you, and under the CBN's 2021 framework escrowed funds are invested in treasury bills so they are returned with any accruable interest. You cannot spend it on hardware, rent, or salaries while it sits in escrow. The paid-up capital, by contrast, is genuinely yours to deploy in the business once you are licensed. Both must be "unencumbered" — not borrowed and not subject to any lien.
Note that figures here reflect the CBN's published categorisations as updated through 2026, and recent guidance has raised the PSSP share-capital bar above the original 2020/2021 level. Because sources have at times conflicted on the exact PSSP figure, confirm the current number against the latest CBN circular before you budget.

Compliance with Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Data Privacy
Compliance is not a box you tick once. It is built into your software, your reporting calendar, and your daily operations, and it answers to two masters: the CBN and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC).
Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA), a fintech that processes personal data above the prescribed threshold — broadly, the data of more than 200 data subjects within six months — is classified as a Data Controller of Major Importance (DCMI) and grouped into a corresponding compliance class. A DCMI must register with the NDPC, appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO), and file annual Compliance Audit Returns. The NDPC's General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID), issued on 20 March 2025 and effective from 19 September 2025, sets out the current procedural detail. The annual audit duty attaches to DCMIs specifically, not automatically to every licensed entity — but most active fintechs cross the threshold quickly.
The compliance pillars every fintech should expect to build:
KYC (Know Your Customer): Tiered verification — BVN, NIN, and address checks — scaled to transaction limits.
Transaction Monitoring: Automated systems that flag patterns suggesting money laundering or terrorism financing.
NDPA Compliance: Customer data encrypted, stored securely (preferably within Nigeria), and processed only with a lawful basis such as explicit consent.
Reporting Obligations: Regular filings to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) and the CBN on large or suspicious transactions.
Projected Legal and Regulatory Filing Costs
Beyond the escrowed deposit, launching a fintech carries real upfront cost in government fees and professional services. The paid-up capital is the biggest line item, but the administrative fees are non-refundable, so budget for them from day one. The CBN's own charges are fixed; the professional-services figures below are market estimates that swing on complexity.

To put it concretely: a PSSP applicant should plan for roughly ₦250 million in paid-up capital, a separate ₦100 million refundable escrow, the ₦100,000 application fee, ₦1 million licensing fee on approval, and somewhere around ₦5–15 million in professional fees on top.
Nigeria as a Regulatory Path for African Fintech
Founders building for the wider continent often treat Nigeria as the template. Its payment-system framework — four-plus licence categories supervised directly by the CBN as OFIs under BOFIA 2020 — is one of Africa's most clearly codified, which is why a Nigerian licence is frequently the first regulatory milestone for platforms with pan-African ambitions. The discipline the CBN demands on capital, escrow, and AML maps closely onto what other regulators across the region expect, so a clean Nigerian build tends to travel well.
Common Misconceptions
"One licence covers everything." It does not. The CBN restricts combining Switching and Processing with MMO activities in a single entity — those two must sit under a CBN-licensed Payment Service Holding Company. By contrast, the PSS-category licences (PSSP, PTSP, and Super Agent) can be combined in one company. So the bar is specific, not blanket.
"The escrow deposit is money you lose." No. The escrow is refunded — with any accruable interest — once the licence is granted or the application is rejected. What stays in the business is your paid-up share capital. The escrow is a temporary lodgement, not a fee and not spendable.
"CAC registration alone lets me start." Incorporating with the Corporate Affairs Commission does not authorise you to process financial transactions. Operating without the relevant CBN licence can get your accounts frozen and expose you to criminal prosecution.
FAQ
How long does it take to get a fintech licence in Nigeria?
Plan for 6 to 18 months. That window covers preparing the application, the CBN's internal review for the AIP, and the final inspection of your physical office and IT infrastructure. Well-prepared applicants with a clean MEMART objects clause and complete policy documents move through the front of that range.
Can a foreign company own a Nigerian fintech?
Yes. Foreign ownership is permitted, but the company must be incorporated locally in Nigeria. The CBN assesses the fitness of foreign directors and requires evidence of capital importation via a Certificate of Capital Importation (CCI).
What is the difference between a PSSP and a PTSP?
A PSSP (Payment Solution Service Provider) handles digital gateways and web-based processing. A PTSP (Payment Terminal Service Provider) handles physical hardware — the deployment and maintenance of Point-of-Sale (PoS) terminals.
Do I need a physical office for a digital bank?
Yes. Even a "digital" bank needs a physical head office where the CBN can conduct onsite inspections and where corporate records are kept.
When to Hire a Lawyer
The CBN's framework is technical and unforgiving of sloppy paperwork. Bring in a specialised fintech lawyer when:
You are choosing a licence tier and want to avoid over-capitalising — picking a PSSP when a Super Agent would do, or vice versa, is an expensive error.
You are drafting the MEMART objects clause to meet CBN standards, the single most common cause of AIP queries.
You need to structure a Payment Service Holding Company to run Switching and MMO activities together.
You are arranging foreign capital importation and the supporting CCI.
You are responding to CBN queries during the AIP phase.
Next Steps
Pin down your core product: Are you moving money (MMO), processing it (PSSP), running terminals (PTSP), or lending it (MFB)? This single decision sets your capital bill.
Secure funding for both sums: Have your full paid-up share capital and the separate refundable escrow ready.
Incorporate your entity: Register with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) with the appropriate share capital and a CBN-ready objects clause.
Draft your policies: Prepare your AML/CFT, KYC, and cybersecurity frameworks before you apply.
Apply for AIP: Submit your formal application and escrow deposit to the Central Bank of Nigeria .

CAC Registration for Payment Service Providers (PSPs) in Nigeria: CBN & Legal Compliance (2026)
CAC Registration for Payment Service Providers (PSPs) in Nigeria: CBN & Legal Compliance (2026)
Nigeria's digital economy is experiencing an unprecedented boom, driven by a youthful, tech-savvy population and a rapidly expanding mobile penetration. At the heart of this revolution are Payment Service Providers (PSPs) – innovative companies that facilitate seamless financial transactions, bridging the gap between traditional banking and the everyday digital lives of millions. As we look towards 2026, the landscape for PSPs in Nigeria continues to evolve, marked by dynamic regulatory frameworks designed to foster innovation while ensuring stability, security, and consumer protection.
For any aspiring or existing PSP looking to thrive in this vibrant market, understanding and meticulously adhering to the foundational legal and regulatory requirements is not just a recommendation, but a cornerstone of sustainable operation. This comprehensive guide from CAC Register Nigeria is tailored to demystify the critical processes of Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) registration and Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) licensing, alongside other vital legal compliance considerations for Payment Service Providers operating in Nigeria, with a forward-looking perspective towards 2026.
From the initial step of incorporating your business to navigating the stringent licensing conditions set by the CBN, this article will serve as your essential roadmap. We will delve into the specific requirements, highlight potential challenges, and offer best practices to ensure your PSP is not only legally compliant but also strategically positioned for success in Nigeria's competitive FinTech space. Whether you're a startup or an established entity planning expansion, robust compliance is your passport to trust, credibility, and long-term growth.
Understanding the Nigerian Payment Ecosystem and PSPs
Nigeria's payment ecosystem is one of the most dynamic and rapidly evolving in Africa. Fueled by a large unbanked and underbanked population, coupled with increasing smartphone penetration, the demand for accessible, efficient, and secure digital payment solutions has skyrocketed. PSPs have emerged as crucial enablers of financial inclusion, driving innovation in areas like mobile payments, online remittances, agent banking, and digital wallets.
In the Nigerian context, Payment Service Providers encompass a broad range of entities that facilitate payment transactions. These can include:
Payment Gateways: Services that authorize and process credit card or direct payments for e-businesses, online retailers, and traditional businesses.
Mobile Money Operators (MMOs): Companies that provide financial services through mobile phone networks, often targeting individuals without traditional bank accounts.
Switching Companies: Entities that provide the infrastructure to connect various payment systems and financial institutions, enabling interoperability.
Payment Solution Service Providers (PSSPs): Offering payment solutions, including payment gateway services, payment processing, and aggregation.
Payment Terminal Service Providers (PTSPs): Deploying and managing Point-of-Sale (POS) terminals for merchants.
Super Agents: Companies that onboard, train, and manage a network of agents to deliver financial services.
Payment Initiation Service Providers (PISPs): Services that initiate a payment order from a user's account with their consent.
Account Information Service Providers (AISPs): Services that access and consolidate information from a user's accounts across different financial institutions with their consent.
The role of these PSPs extends beyond mere transaction processing; they are instrumental in fostering economic growth, reducing reliance on cash, and creating a more inclusive financial landscape for all Nigerians.
The Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) and Its Foundational Role
Before a PSP can even think about obtaining a license from the Central Bank of Nigeria, it must first establish its legal identity as a legitimate business entity. This foundational step is handled by the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), the statutory body responsible for regulating the formation and management of companies in Nigeria.
The CAC's mandate, primarily derived from the Companies and Allied Matters Act (CAMA) 2020, is to:
Administer CAMA, including the registration of companies, business names, and incorporated trustees.
Regulate the formation, operation, and winding up of companies.
Maintain a register of companies, business names, and incorporated trustees.
Choosing the Right Business Structure for a PSP
While CAMA provides for various business structures, a Limited Liability Company (LLC) is almost universally the preferred, and often mandatory, structure for PSPs in Nigeria. This is because:
Limited Liability: Protects the personal assets of shareholders from business debts and liabilities, which is crucial in a high-risk financial services environment.
Perpetual Succession: The company continues to exist regardless of changes in ownership or management.
Credibility and Trust: An LLC structure often signals a higher level of professionalism and commitment, which is vital for attracting investors, partners, and customers, and is a prerequisite for CBN licensing.
Capital Raising: Easier to raise capital through equity financing by issuing shares.
Basic CAC Registration Requirements for a Limited Liability Company
The process of registering an LLC with the CAC typically involves the following key steps and requirements:
Name Availability Search & Reservation:
The first step is to propose two unique names for your company and conduct an availability search on the CAC portal. If approved, the name is reserved for 60 days, during which you must complete the registration process. The name should ideally reflect the nature of your business (e.g., "XYZ Payments Limited").
Appointing Directors and Shareholders:
A private company must have a minimum of one director and one shareholder (who can be the same person). For PSPs, the CBN often has specific requirements regarding the number and qualifications of directors, including independent directors and those with relevant financial sector experience. Directors must be at least 18 years old, of sound mind, and not disqualified under CAMA.
Defining Share Capital:
This is critical for PSPs. While CAMA permits a minimum authorized share capital, the Central Bank of Nigeria mandates significantly higher minimum share capital requirements for different PSP license categories (which we will discuss later). It is prudent to incorporate with an authorized share capital that meets or exceeds the CBN's requirements for your intended license category from the outset.
Registered Address:
A physical address in Nigeria must be provided as the company's registered office.
Company Secretary:
A private company may or may not appoint a company secretary at the point of incorporation, but it is highly recommended, especially for companies seeking CBN licensing. A public company must have a company secretary.
Memorandum and Articles of Association (MEMART):
These are the foundational documents governing the company. The Memorandum outlines the company's objects (what the company is formed to do), its share capital, and liability. The Articles of Association define the internal management rules. For PSPs, the objects must explicitly state the intention to operate as a payment service provider and engage in related financial activities.
Means of Identification:
Valid means of identification (e.g., National ID Card, International Passport, Driver's License, NIN) for all directors, shareholders, and company secretary.
Proficiency and Professional Bodies (Optional but Recommended):
While not strictly a CAC requirement, having directors and management with relevant professional qualifications (e.g., CIBN, ICAN, ACCA) and experience in finance or technology adds significant credibility and eases the CBN licensing process.
Once all documents are prepared, they are filed electronically through the CAC online portal. Upon successful submission and payment of requisite fees, the CAC will issue a Certificate of Incorporation, a Certified True Copy (CTC) of the MEMART, and the Status Report of the Company. This marks the successful legal birth of your PSP in Nigeria.
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) and PSP Regulation
While CAC registration provides the legal corporate identity, it is the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) that grants the authority to operate as a Payment Service Provider. The CBN is the apex financial regulatory body in Nigeria, responsible for maintaining monetary stability, ensuring a sound financial system, and regulating all financial institutions, including PSPs.
The CBN's regulatory framework for PSPs is robust and continually updated to address emerging technologies, market risks, and global best practices. Key regulatory instruments and guidelines include:
Guidelines on Licensing and Regulation of Payment Service Banks (PSBs): For entities that combine features of traditional banks with mobile money operations.
Regulations on Mobile Money Services in Nigeria: Governing the operation of mobile money schemes.
Guidelines for the Operations of Payment System Banks in Nigeria.
Regulatory Framework for Open Banking in Nigeria: Facilitating secure data sharing between financial institutions and third-party service providers.
Revised Guidelines for Licensing and Regulation of Payment Service Providers in Nigeria (often updated): This is the most critical document, outlining the various license categories and their specific requirements.
Interplay Between CAC Registration and CBN Licensing
It is crucial to understand that CAC registration is a prerequisite for CBN licensing. You cannot apply for a CBN license without first having a duly incorporated company. The CBN expects to see a legally formed entity with clear corporate governance structures in place before considering its application to operate in the sensitive financial services sector.
Navigating CBN Licensing for PSPs (Post-CAC Registration)
The CBN categorizes PSPs based on the scope and nature of services they intend to offer. Each category comes with distinct minimum share capital requirements, which are subject to periodic review by the CBN. As of current guidelines (and anticipating continuity into 2026), these are some of the key categories and their associated capital requirements:
Switching and Processing License:
Minimum Share Capital: N2 Billion (Two Billion Naira).
Scope: Provides infrastructure for routing and processing transactions between financial institutions, payment gateways, and other payment service providers. Often considered the backbone of the payment system.
Mobile Money Operator (MMO) License:
Minimum Share Capital: N2 Billion (Two Billion Naira).
Scope: Enables the provision of financial services through mobile phones, including wallets, remittances, bill payments, and agent networks.
Payment Solution Service Provider (PSSP) License:
Minimum Share Capital: N250 Million (Two Hundred and Fifty Million Naira).
Scope: Offers payment gateway services, payment processing, and aggregation services. This is a common entry point for many online payment businesses.
Payment Terminal Service Provider (PTSP) License:
Minimum Share Capital: N100 Million (One Hundred Million Naira).
Scope: Engages in the deployment, maintenance, and support of Point-of-Sale (POS) terminals.
Super Agent License:
Minimum Share Capital: N50 Million (Fifty Million Naira).
Scope: Manages a network of agents to provide financial services on behalf of financial institutions and mobile money operators.
Payment Initiation Service Provider (PISP) & Account Information Service Provider (AISP) License (under Open Banking Framework):
Minimum Share Capital: N50 Million (Fifty Million Naira).
Scope: PISPs initiate payments directly from customer accounts, while AISPs aggregate account information. These are newer categories driven by open banking initiatives.
It is imperative to confirm the latest capital requirements directly from the CBN's official guidelines, as these figures are subject to change.

The CBN Licensing Application Process
The CBN licensing process is rigorous and typically involves two main stages: Approval-in-Principle (AIP) and Final License Issuance.
Pre-Requisites and Documentation for AIP:
Formal Application Letter: Addressed to the Director, Payments System Management Department, CBN.
Certificate of Incorporation: From CAC.
Certified True Copy (CTC) of MEMART: Clearly stating the objects of the company align with PSP operations.
Evidence of Minimum Share Capital: A statement of affairs from a reputable bank, showing that the required share capital has been paid up and is held in an escrow account with the CBN.
Detailed Business Plan: Outlining the company's vision, mission, products/services, target market, operational model, financial projections (for at least 3-5 years), and marketing strategy.
Technology Risk Management Framework: Details of the IT infrastructure, security protocols, disaster recovery plan, business continuity plan, and data protection measures.
Risk Management Policies: Covering operational risk, credit risk, market risk, and compliance risk.
Anti-Money Laundering (AML) / Combating Financing of Terrorism (CFT) Policy: Comprehensive policies and procedures for KYC (Know Your Customer), transaction monitoring, and suspicious activity reporting.
Corporate Governance Framework: Details of board composition, roles, responsibilities, and internal controls.
Profiles of Board of Directors and Key Management Staff: Including their résumés, professional qualifications, experience, and regulatory clearances (e.g., from CBN for fit and proper persons).
Organizational Structure: A detailed chart showing reporting lines.
Shareholding Structure: Details of all significant shareholders.
Feasibility Study Report: Demonstrating the viability of the proposed PSP business.
Payment of Application Fees.
CBN Due Diligence and Review:
The CBN conducts thorough due diligence on all submitted documents, the proposed directors, management, and the business model. This may involve meetings, interviews, and on-site inspections.
Approval-in-Principle (AIP):
If satisfied, the CBN issues an AIP, which grants conditional approval to proceed with setting up operations. The AIP typically has a validity period (e.g., 6 months) within which the PSP must meet all conditions for final licensing.
Conditions for Final License Issuance (Post-AIP):
During the AIP period, the PSP must fulfill various conditions, which often include:
Setting up the required IT infrastructure and obtaining necessary certifications (e.g., PCI DSS for card processing).
Recruiting and onboarding key personnel.
Developing and testing all systems and processes.
Submission of audited financial statements (if applicable).
Demonstration of readiness for operations through a pre-go-live inspection by the CBN.
Final License Issuance:
Upon successful fulfillment of all AIP conditions, the CBN grants the final operating license. This license is typically renewed periodically and is subject to ongoing compliance with CBN regulations.
Key Legal and Compliance Considerations for PSPs (Beyond CAC & CBN)
Operating a PSP in Nigeria requires adherence to a broader spectrum of laws and regulations beyond just CAC and CBN. Neglecting these can lead to significant penalties, reputational damage, and even license revocation.
1. Data Protection: Nigeria Data Protection Act (NDPA) 2023
The NDPA (which replaced the NDPR) is critical for PSPs, given the sensitive nature of customer financial and personal data they handle. PSPs must:
Appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO).
Implement robust data security measures to prevent breaches.
Obtain explicit consent for data processing.
Ensure data localization (where required) and adherence to cross-border data transfer rules.
Provide mechanisms for data subjects to exercise their rights (e.g., right to access, rectification, erasure).
2. Anti-Money Laundering (AML) / Combating Financing of Terrorism (CFT)
PSPs are designated non-financial institutions (DNFI) or financial institutions, subject to stringent AML/CFT regulations under the Money Laundering (Prohibition) Act and the Terrorism (Prevention) Act. Key requirements include:
KYC/CDD (Customer Due Diligence): Implementing robust procedures to identify and verify customers.
Transaction Monitoring: Systems to detect and report suspicious transactions.
Reporting: Filing Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) and Currency Transaction Reports (CTRs) to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU).
SCUML Registration: Registering with the Special Control Unit Against Money Laundering (SCUML) is mandatory for many PSP categories.
Employee Training: Regular training for staff on AML/CFT policies and procedures.
3. Consumer Protection
The CBN's Consumer Protection Framework and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act (FCCPA) protect consumers from unfair practices. PSPs must ensure:
Transparency in pricing, terms, and conditions.
Fair and prompt resolution of customer complaints.
Protection of customer funds and data.
Clear communication regarding service availability and downtime.
4. Cybersecurity
Given the digital nature of PSPs, cybersecurity is paramount. The CBN issues guidelines on cybersecurity for financial institutions, and PSPs must:
Implement robust cybersecurity frameworks and technologies.
Conduct regular vulnerability assessments and penetration testing.
Have incident response plans in place.
Adhere to standards like ISO 27001 and PCI DSS (if processing card data).
5. Taxation
PSPs are subject to various taxes at federal and state levels, including:
Company Income Tax (CIT): Levied on profits.
Value Added Tax (VAT): On goods and services.
Withholding Tax (WHT): On certain payments (e.g., rent, dividends, services).
Stamp Duties: On certain legal documents and transactions.
Pay As You Earn (PAYE): For employee salaries.
Education Tax.
National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) Levy.
Obtaining a Tax Identification Number (TIN) from the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS) is an early post-incorporation step.
6. Contract Law
All service agreements, terms and conditions, partnerships, and vendor contracts must be legally sound and compliant with Nigerian contract law.
Challenges and Best Practices for PSPs in Nigeria (2026 Outlook)
While the opportunities are immense, PSPs in Nigeria face unique challenges. Understanding these and adopting best practices will be crucial for success in 2026 and beyond.
Challenges:
Evolving Regulatory Landscape: The CBN frequently updates its guidelines, requiring PSPs to stay agile and constantly adapt their operations.
High Capital Requirements: The significant minimum share capital for some licenses can be a barrier to entry for startups.
Infrastructure Limitations: Inconsistent internet connectivity, power supply issues, and varying levels of digital literacy in rural areas can impact service delivery.
Cybersecurity Threats: The increasing sophistication of cyberattacks poses a continuous threat to financial systems and customer data.
Talent Acquisition: Finding and retaining skilled FinTech professionals, especially in areas like cybersecurity, data science, and compliance, remains a challenge.
Competition: The market is becoming increasingly crowded with both local and international players.
Foreign Exchange Volatility: Affects operational costs and international transactions for PSPs dealing with cross-border payments.
Best Practices:
Proactive Regulatory Engagement: Stay abreast of all CBN, CAC, and other relevant regulatory updates. Consider joining industry associations that lobby for favourable policies and provide compliance insights.
Robust Compliance Framework: Embed compliance into your organizational DNA. Develop comprehensive internal policies, conduct regular audits, and invest in compliance software.
Strong Corporate Governance: Establish a competent and diverse board of directors, implement clear internal controls, and foster a culture of ethics and accountability.
Continuous Innovation: Leverage emerging technologies (AI, blockchain, biometrics) to offer differentiated services, improve efficiency, and enhance security.
Strategic Partnerships: Collaborate with traditional financial institutions, telecommunication companies, and other FinTech players to expand reach and offer integrated solutions.
Focus on Customer Experience and Security: Prioritize user-friendly interfaces, efficient customer support, and impregnable security measures to build trust and loyalty.
Investment in Talent: Attract and retain top talent through competitive compensation, continuous learning opportunities, and a vibrant work culture.
Scalable Technology Infrastructure: Build systems that can handle increasing transaction volumes and adapt to future technological advancements.
Conclusion
The journey to becoming a fully compliant and successful Payment Service Provider in Nigeria is multifaceted, demanding meticulous attention to legal and regulatory requirements. From the foundational Corporate Affairs Commission registration to the stringent licensing process orchestrated by the Central Bank of Nigeria, every step is critical. As Nigeria's digital economy continues its upward trajectory towards 2026, the demand for innovative and reliable payment solutions will only intensify.
For aspiring and existing PSPs, navigating this complex landscape requires more than just a brilliant business idea; it demands a deep understanding of the regulatory environment, a commitment to compliance, and a proactive approach to risk management. By adhering to the guidelines outlined in this article, PSPs can not only secure their operational legitimacy but also build a foundation of trust and resilience that is essential for long-term success.

Nigeria Fintech in 2026: OPay, Moniepoint, PalmPay, Kuda and the Market Map
Nigeria is Africa's most funded fintech market and its most demanding one. Two unicorns are preparing for public markets, the regulator has handed the largest players national licences, and the naira has rewritten every dollar valuation. This is where the market stands, company by company, with the figures sourced.
MobiBank Editorial
·
October 9, 2026
·
12 min read
The short answer
Nigerian fintech in 2026 is a market of a few very large agent and merchant networks, now regulated like banks and heading for listings.
OPay is implied at around $3.1 billion by its shareholder Opera and is reported to be exploring a US listing near $4 billion. Moniepoint is a unicorn that raised a $200 million Series C. PalmPay is reported to be raising at a valuation above $1 billion with a Hong Kong listing in view. Kuda cut its losses by 84% in 2024. In January 2026 the Central Bank of Nigeria upgraded all of them to national microfinance licences.
For an investor, Nigeria is two stories at once. The demand side is enormous and still growing: tens of millions of adults moving from cash to digital payments, a payments system processing quadrillions of naira, and remittances above $21 billion a year. The supply side is consolidating fast, around a handful of operators who won the cash-in, cash-out network on the street. The interesting question in 2026 is not whether Nigerian fintech is large. It is who owns the next layer.
$214M
Equity raised by Nigerian startups in H1 2026, the most of any African country (Africa: The Big Deal)
15.7B
Point-of-sale transactions in Nigeria in 2025, up 19.8% (Central Bank of Nigeria 2025 Annual Report)
$21.8B
Diaspora remittances into Nigeria in 2025, flat on 2024 (CBN data reported by Vanguard)
The Players
The market map, company by company
The four names that dominate Nigerian consumer and merchant fintech share one feature: each built or bought physical distribution. A Nigerian payments brand wins on the street, through agents and terminals in shops, before it wins in an app store. The figures below are the latest publicly reported, with the date and source for each.
OPay IPO talk

Moniepoint Unicorn

PalmPay Raising

Next step Hong Kong listing explored
Kuda Restructuring

Sources: The Condia and WeeTracker on Opera's filing (Apr 2026); ThisDay citing Bloomberg (May 2026); TechCabal and Techpoint (Oct 2025); Bloomberg (Aug 2026); Nairametrics (Sep 2025); BusinessDay on Kuda's audited accounts (Jan 2026).
OPay: the largest network, priced through a shareholder
OPay has not raised a priced round since 2021, when SoftBank's Vision Fund 2 led a $400 million round at about $2 billion. Its most useful valuation signal is indirect: Opera, which holds 9.7%, valued that stake at $294.6 million in an April 2026 securities filing, which implies roughly $3.1 billion for the whole company. Bloomberg has since reported that OPay is working with Citigroup, Deutsche Bank and JPMorgan on a possible US listing at around $4 billion. That is a report, not a filing, and should be read as such.
The operating scale behind the number is real: more than 50 million users in Nigeria, monthly transaction volume reported above $12 billion, and an agent network of more than 500,000. OPay reportedly reached its first monthly profit in 2024.
Moniepoint: the merchant terminal company that became a bank
Moniepoint crossed a $1 billion valuation in October 2024 on a $110 million first close of its Series C, led by Development Partners International with Google's Africa Investment Fund among the investors. A $90 million extension in October 2025 brought the Series C to $200 million, with LeapFrog anchoring the close and IFC, Visa, Proparco and Swedfund participating. No new valuation was disclosed.
Its own 2025 review describes more than 6 million businesses served and claims that 8 in 10 in-person payments in Nigeria run on a Moniepoint terminal. Revenue figures for 2025 circulate in a range from about $265 million to $600 million, but none is audited and we do not repeat them as fact. In August 2026 the company began phasing out its UK remittance product to refocus on Nigeria and Kenya, where it completed a 78% stake in a microfinance bank.
PalmPay: the handset-backed challenger
PalmPay's distinctive asset is its shareholder base: Transsion, maker of the Tecno, Infinix and itel phones that dominate the African handset market, alongside NetEase and MediaTek. It reported more than 40 million users in September 2025 and was ranked the top fintech in the Financial Times list of Africa's fastest-growing companies that year. In August 2026 Bloomberg reported it was in talks to raise around $200 million at a valuation above $1 billion and preparing for a possible Hong Kong listing. The round had not closed at the time of the report.
Kuda: the neobank that chose profitability
Kuda was the poster child of Nigerian digital banking in 2021, valued at $500 million after a $55 million Series B. Its audited 2024 accounts tell the story of the years since. The loss fell 84% to $5.83 million, operating expenses fell 61%, and registered customers grew to 7 million. Revenue in dollars fell 15%, while revenue at its Nigerian subsidiary nearly doubled in naira. The company restructured again with layoffs in March 2026.
Kuda's naira revenue nearly doubled in 2024 while its dollar revenue fell 15%. That single line explains most Nigerian fintech valuations.
The rest of the map
Beyond the four consumer leaders, the infrastructure layer is consolidating. Flutterwave raised a Series E in June 2026 at a reported $3.2 billion with Ripple among the investors, and acquired the open banking company Mono. Paystack , owned by Stripe, reorganised under a holding company after reaching group profitability and became a microfinance bank in January 2026. Paga reported $11 billion processed across 169 million transactions in 2025 and became PayPal's entry point into Nigeria. LemFi raised a $53 million Series B in January 2025 for diaspora remittances. Interswitch , valued at $1 billion when Visa took a stake in 2019, still has no listing date.
The Money
How much capital is going into Nigerian fintech
Funding trackers count differently, so their totals should never be compared with each other, only within the same series. On Partech's count, Nigerian startups raised $520 million in equity in 2024, up 11%, across 103 deals, the most of any African country. On Africa: The Big Deal's count, Nigeria raised $254 million in total in the first half of 2026, second to Egypt, but led the continent on equity with $214 million.
Across Africa as a whole, Partech counted $4.1 billion raised in 2025, up 25%, with fintech at $1.49 billion. Fintech remains the single largest category on every tracker, at around 40% of African startup funding.
The Currency
Why every dollar valuation in Nigeria needs a footnote
The official naira rate moved from about ₦462 per dollar in June 2023 to ₦1,535 at the end of 2024, a loss of roughly 70% of its dollar value in eighteen months. It recovered partially to about ₦1,450 at the end of 2025 and around ₦1,332 in early October 2026.
For a company that earns in naira and is valued in dollars, that is the dominant variable. A business can double its local revenue and still report a decline to a foreign investor, which is exactly what Kuda's accounts show. It also explains why the leaders that held their valuations are the ones with the largest transaction volumes, where scale outran the currency, and why several have built dollar-earning lines such as remittances. Any valuation comparison across 2021, 2024 and 2026 is partly a currency comparison.
The Regulator
What changed in regulation between 2024 and 2026
Identity enforcement From March 2024 the Central Bank of Nigeria required every account and wallet to be linked to a Bank Verification Number or National Identification Number, with unlinked accounts restricted.
The onboarding freeze Between 29 April and 3 June 2024 the CBN stopped OPay, Moniepoint, Kuda, PalmPay and Paga from onboarding new customers until they tightened address and facial verification and blocked peer-to-peer crypto transfers.
National licences In January 2026 the same five were upgraded to national microfinance licences covering all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. Supervision now looks much more like bank supervision.
Bank recapitalisation New minimum capital for commercial banks, announced in March 2024, carried a 31 March 2026 deadline. The banks that complete it will be better capitalised competitors and partners for fintechs.
Open banking Nigeria issued Africa's first open banking operational guidelines in 2023. The planned August 2025 go-live slipped, and the CBN set out a phased rollout through 2026. Whether the rail is fully live should be checked at the time of reading.
The Opportunity
What is still unsolved
The 2023 EFInA Access to Financial Services survey found 64% of Nigerian adults formally financially included, up from 56% in 2020, and 26% fully excluded, roughly 40 million adults. The urban-rural gap was still 20 percentage points.
That remaining population is the hardest to reach with the model that won the first round. Agent networks need cash logistics, terminals need power and a data signal, and app-based products need a smartphone with data. The next layer of growth in Nigeria is likely to come from products that keep working when one of those inputs is missing, and from distribution that does not assume a city.
Where We Sit
MobiBank and Nigeria
MobiBank is a Finnish financial technology company building a mobile banking platform for markets where connectivity and infrastructure cannot be assumed, including a patented channel that allows the service to work without internet access. Nigeria is the first market in our Africa rollout, and we have published our partnership and deployment plans on this site.
MobiBank is not yet licensed in Nigeria and does not offer accounts there today. Certain capabilities described across this site remain under development, and the licensing route is still being finalised.
Common Questions
Frequently asked questions
What is the biggest fintech company in Nigeria?
By users and implied valuation, OPay. Its shareholder Opera valued its 9.7% stake at $294.6 million in April 2026, implying about $3.1 billion, and OPay reports more than 50 million users in Nigeria and over 500,000 agents. Moniepoint is the largest by merchant payments, claiming that 8 in 10 in-person payments in Nigeria run on its terminals. Flutterwave, reported at $3.2 billion in June 2026, is the largest in business payments infrastructure.
What is OPay's valuation in 2026?
About $3.1 billion on an implied basis. Opera disclosed in an April 2026 filing that its 9.7% stake was worth $294.6 million. OPay's last priced round was $400 million at around $2 billion in 2021. Bloomberg reported in 2026 that OPay is working with banks on a possible US listing at about $4 billion, which is a report rather than a filed offering.
What is Moniepoint's valuation?
The public figure is above $1 billion, set when Moniepoint became a unicorn in October 2024 on the first close of its Series C. A $90 million extension in October 2025 brought the Series C to $200 million, with investors including DPI, LeapFrog, IFC, Google and Visa, but no updated valuation was disclosed.
Is PalmPay going public?
It is reported to be preparing. In August 2026 Bloomberg reported that PalmPay was in talks to raise around $200 million at a valuation above $1 billion and was exploring a Hong Kong listing, with no banks or timetable set. PalmPay is backed by Transsion, NetEase and MediaTek and reported more than 40 million users in September 2025.
Is Kuda Bank profitable?
Not on a full-year basis in its latest audited accounts. Kuda's 2024 loss was $5.83 million, down 84% from $35.11 million in 2023, after operating expenses were cut by 61%. Revenue at its Nigerian subsidiary nearly doubled in naira while group revenue fell 15% in dollars because of the currency. Full-year 2025 results had not been published at the time of writing.
How much did Nigerian fintech startups raise in 2025 and 2026?
It depends on the tracker. Partech counted $520 million of equity into Nigerian startups in 2024, the most in Africa. Africa: The Big Deal counted $254 million into Nigerian startups in the first half of 2026, with $214 million of that as equity, again the most in Africa. Fintech accounts for roughly 40% of African startup funding on every major tracker. Figures from different trackers use different methods and should not be compared directly.
Is Nigeria a good market for fintech investment?
It is the largest and most competitive fintech market in Africa, with deep demand and a regulator that has become stricter and more bank-like since 2024. The main risks are currency, since the naira lost roughly 70% of its dollar value between mid-2023 and end-2024, and regulatory change. The main opportunity is the roughly 40 million adults still financially excluded, who are hardest to reach with app-only and terminal-dependent models. This is general information, not investment advice.
What licences do Nigerian fintechs need?
It depends on the activity. Consumer players that hold deposits typically operate as microfinance banks, and in January 2026 the Central Bank of Nigeria upgraded OPay, Moniepoint, Kuda, PalmPay and Paga to national microfinance licences covering the whole country. Payments-only businesses use payment service licences, and agent networks fall under the CBN's agent banking guidelines. Every account must be linked to a BVN or NIN.
