Nigeria earns more from remittances but pays more on foreign investments
Published
4 hours ago on
October 29, 2026
By
Tunde Adekola
Nigeria recorded higher inflows from diaspora remittances in the second quarter of 2026, but the gains were partly offset by rising payments on foreign investments, highlighting competing pressures on the country’s external accounts.
The secondary income account surplus rose to $6.30 billion in the second quarter of 2026, from $5.47 billion in the preceding quarter, largely driven by a 10 percent increase in diaspora remittance inflows to $5.82 billion.
However, the primary income account deficit widened to $4.20 billion from $3.23 billion in the first quarter, reflecting higher interest payments on portfolio investment liabilities and increased earnings accruing to non-resident investors.
The figures highlight the dual impact of international financial flows on Nigeria’s external position, with remittances providing a significant source of foreign exchange while payments on foreign investments and external loans contributed to higher income outflows.
According to the Central Bank’s report, the improvement in the secondary income account reflected sustained gains from the Central Bank of Nigeria’s ongoing reforms, particularly the narrowing spread between the official and parallel exchange rates, which reduced the incentive to route remittances through informal markets.
General government transfers also increased to $530 million in the second quarter, from $220 million in the preceding quarter, further supporting the secondary income surplus.
On the other hand, the deficit in the investment income sub-account widened to $4.50 billion from $3.47 billion in the first quarter, driven mainly by a higher deficit in portfolio investment income, which increased by 20.3 percent to $2.49 billion.
Interest payments on short-term instruments held by non-resident investors rose to $2.11 billion from $1.90 billion, while payments on long-term debt securities increased to $480 million from $190 million.
The deficit in direct investment income also widened to $1.82 billion from $1.40 billion, reflecting higher reinvested earnings accruing to non-resident investors, which rose to $900 million from $780 million.
At the same time, earnings on residents’ direct investments abroad fell to $110 million from $430 million, contributing to the widening deficit.
Dividend payments to non-resident investors moderated slightly to $1.02 billion from $1.04 billion, while income on reserve assets declined to $530 million from $570 million.
The deficit in other investment income also widened to $710 million from $630 million, reflecting higher interest payments on external loan liabilities. However, the surplus in the compensation of employees sub-account increased to $300 million from $240 million in the preceding quarter.
Beyond the income accounts, Nigeria recorded a higher net foreign exchange inflow of $21.09 billion in the second quarter, compared with $20.30 billion in the first quarter, supported by a decline in aggregate foreign exchange outflows.
Total foreign exchange inflows fell by 4.24 percent to $30.03 billion from $31.36 billion, while outflows declined by 19.17 percent to $8.94 billion from $11.06 billion.
Foreign exchange inflows through the Central Bank fell by 20.47 percent to $8.12 billion from $10.21 billion, while inflows through autonomous sources increased by 3.59 percent to $21.91 billion from $21.15 billion.
Consequently, autonomous sources recorded a net inflow of $17.74 billion, compared with $17.53 billion in the first quarter. The Central Bank’s net inflow also increased to $3.35 billion from $2.77 billion.
Meanwhile, average turnover at the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market declined by 7.56 percent to $530.42 million from $573.81 million in the preceding quarter.
The average exchange rate of the naira strengthened to N1,365.95 per dollar in the second quarter from N1,384.48 in the first quarter, representing a 1.36 percent appreciation during the review period.
The performance of other emerging-market currencies was mixed during the quarter. The Chinese renminbi and Russian ruble appreciated by 1.74 percent and 5.33 percent, respectively, supported by export earnings and other market factors, while the South African rand depreciated by 0.79 percent amid global risk aversion linked to uncertainty in the Middle East and domestic concerns over anti-immigration demonstrations. Nigeria’s portfolio investment inflows surge to $7.09 billion as direct investment lags
Published
2 days ago on
October 27, 2026
By
Kemi Adelabu
Nigeria’s portfolio investment inflows rose 17.6% quarter-on-quarter to $7.09 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up from $6.03 billion in the first quarter (Q1) , according to the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN).
The CBN attributed the $1.06 billion increase to higher inflows into long-term general government debt securities in its Q2 2026 Economic Report published on Monday, October 26.
The figures indicate that portfolio investment remained the largest component of new financial liabilities recorded in the quarter, outpacing direct investment liabilities as other investment liabilities also increased.
Portfolio inflows rise to $7.09 billion
The CBN’s financial-account data showed that portfolio investment inflows increased faster than direct investment liabilities between the first and second quarters of 2026.
The increase was driven by higher inflows into long-term general government debt securities, according to the report.
Portfolio investment inflows rose to $7.09 billion from $6.03 billion in Q1, an increase of $1.06 billion, or 17.6%.
Direct investment liabilities increased to $1.15 billion from $1.03 billion, representing a rise of $120 million, or approximately 11.7%, driven by higher reinvested earnings.
Other investment liabilities climbed to $2.75 billion from $1.36 billion, reflecting higher loan drawdowns by government and other sectors, alongside increased currency and deposit liabilities of deposit-taking corporations.
Net incurrence of financial liabilities increased to $10.84 billion from $8.36 billion in the preceding quarter.
Portfolio investment inflows were approximately six times the size of direct investment liabilities in Q2. Based on these figures, portfolio inflows accounted for about 65% of net liabilities incurred during the quarter, compared with roughly 72% in Q1, as other investment liabilities grew faster.
Nigeria’s FX inflows fall in Q2
The increase in portfolio investment occurred alongside a decline in aggregate foreign exchange inflows during the quarter, according to the CBN report.
Total FX inflows fell 4.24% to $30.03 billion from $31.36 billion in Q1, reflecting different movements in autonomous inflows and receipts through the central bank.
Autonomous FX inflows rose 3.59% to $21.91 billion.
Inflows through the CBN declined 20.47% to $8.12 billion.
Nigeria’s financial account recorded net lending of $1.74 billion, compared with net borrowing of $2.03 billion in Q1, a shift the CBN linked mainly to increased acquisition of other investment and reserve assets.
External reserves rose to $51.39 billion at the end of June from $48.35 billion at the end of March.
The average Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) rate also strengthened to N1,365.95 per dollar from N1,384.48 per dollar in the preceding quarter.
Nigeria’s net international investment liability narrowed to $92.94 billion from $94.68 billion, although total financial liabilities increased by $9.71 billion to $238.66 billion.
Portfolio inflows outpace direct investment
The Q2 figures reinforce the importance of portfolio investment in Nigeria’s recorded financial-account flows, while highlighting the smaller contribution from direct investment liabilities.
Portfolio investments generally involve securities such as government debt instruments, while direct investment measures a different category of cross-border investment.
The two figures should therefore not be treated as interchangeable measures of foreign capital entering the economy.
The CBN’s balance-of-payments figures are also distinct from the National Bureau of Statistics’ (NBS) capital importation data and should not be interpreted as total capital importation.
While portfolio inflows can support demand for government securities and foreign exchange liquidity, their increase does not necessarily translate into equivalent long-term capital formation.
The composition of inflows, particularly the balance between portfolio and direct investment, remains important when assessing the nature of foreign capital entering Nigeria.(Nairametrics)

How Digital Payments Are Transforming Businesses in Nigeria
Young Nigerians now use different digital tools, from a forex trading app for side investments to instant transfers and mobile wallets for everyday spending.
By
Branded Content
Updated December 10, 2025
Twitter
Add us to your Google feed
If you live in Nigeria today, you already feel it! Money now moves more by phone than by hand. Nigerians pay for groceries, transport, rent, and even school fees with instant transfers. Young Nigerians now use different digital tools, from a forex trading app for side investments to instant transfers and mobile wallets for everyday spending.
Advertisement
This change is not just a feeling. It is backed by hard numbers released in the last few months.
On 3 July 2025, reports noted that Nigeria processed 7.9 billion real-time transactions in 2024, based on data from EnterpriseNGR. That made Nigeria Africa’s leading real-time payments market and placed it among global leaders like India, Brazil, and Thailand. Those 7.9 billion payments represented 2.97% of the entire world’s 266.2 billion real-time transactions in 2024.
Read Also WTO Warns Of ‘Most Serious And Sustained’ Trade Disruptions ›
US, Canada Unable To Reach Trade Pact To Avert Trump Tariffs ›
Brazil Seeks WTO Consultation Over US Tariffs ›
Real-time payments sit inside a much bigger cashless story. On 29 July 2025, new reports citing fresh NIBSS data showed that electronic payment transactions hit ₦284.99 trillion in Q1 2025. That was a 17.7% increase over the ₦234.49 trillion recorded in Q1 2024. Point-of-sale (PoS) payments alone reached ₦10.45 trillion in that same quarter, more than double the ₦3.62 trillion seen a year earlier.
The report also highlighted how quickly PoS terminals are spreading. In January 2025, there were 5.5 million active PoS terminals in Nigeria. By March 2025, that number had risen to 5.9 million. In the same months of 2024, only about 2.4–2.6 million terminals were active. That means more physical touchpoints for digital money in markets, motor parks, and small shops.
Advertisement
The growth is not only in one quarter. NIBSS data, summarised in an August 2025 insight note, showed that total electronic payments in Nigeria reached around ₦1.07 quadrillion in 2024, the highest level ever recorded. Another analysis of the same NIBSS figures noted that about 11.2 billion e-payment transactions were processed in 2024, a rise of more than 15% year-on-year.
Real-time rails are doing most of the heavy lifting. A payment trends review published in June 2025 using ACI Worldwide data found that NIBSS Instant Payments (NIP), launched back in 2011, accounted for 82.1% of all cashless transactions in Nigeria in 2023. It also estimated that 27.7% of all transactions in the country in 2023 were real-time payments, and projected that this share could reach 50.1% by 2028.
This growth is now being recognised at a continental level. In November 2025, AfricaNenda’s SIIPS 2025 work cited NIP as Africa’s first “mature” instant payment system, and highlighted that instant payments across Africa altogether reached nearly US$2 trillion in value in 2024, with Nigeria as a major contributor.
The macroeconomic impact is also being measured. A December 2024 analysis of Nigeria and South Africa’s real-time payments estimated that in 2023, real-time payments added around US$7 billion to Nigeria’s GDP. It is projected that this contribution could grow to US$15 billion by 2028, assuming adoption continues to deepen. For policymakers and investors, this is no longer just “fintech hype”. It is a measurable part of growth.
Advertisement
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) leaders recently shared updated data. At Nigeria Fintech Week 2025 in Lagos, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), through a representative of Olayemi Cardoso, said that electronic payment volumes increased from 3.9 billion (valued at ₦280 trillion) in August 2024 to 4.12 billion (valued at ₦384 trillion) by July 2025, reflecting growing adoption of digital payment channels
The social side of this shift is visible. More Nigerians now hold formal bank or wallet accounts. NIBSS reported in August 2025 that BVN-linked bank account holders had reached 66.2 million, and that total cashless transaction values had grown from ₦237.11 trillion in Q1 2024 to ₦295 trillion in Q1 2025. That means more people are inside the formal system, able to receive transfers, credits, and remittances directly.
Of course, this path is not smooth. The same NIBSS and media data that celebrate growth also hint at stress points. When monthly breakdowns of NIP usage show dips, like the fall from ₦100.06 trillion in January 2025 to ₦88.87 trillion in February before a recovery in March, analysts link part of this to network pressures and seasonal effects. Nigerians know the lived reality behind those numbers: queues at PoS stands when networks fail, and merchants holding goods while “awaiting alert”.
There are also fraud concerns. As transaction volumes rise into the hundreds of trillions of naira, banks and regulators repeatedly warn the public about fake alerts, phishing links, and social-engineering scams.
Advertisement
The rapid growth in real-time transactions, while positive, leaves less time to detect suspicious activity before money moves. This is why stronger authentication, better user education, and tighter monitoring are recurring themes at fintech conferences and CBN forums. Still, the direction of travel is clear.
In 2023, just over a quarter of Nigeria’s transactions were real-time. By 2028, it may be half. In 2024, Nigeria handled 7.9 billion real-time payments and more than a quadrillion naira in e-payments overall. In Q1 2025 alone, the country processed nearly ₦285 trillion electronically, with PoS volumes more than doubling year-on-year. These are not abstract figures. They describe how Nigerians now pay, save, send, and receive money.
For ordinary citizens, the benefits are straightforward: faster payments, more choice, and often more safety than carrying cash. For businesses, especially SMEs, real-time settlement can improve cash flow and reduce operational risk. For the wider economy, the data now show a clear link between real-time payments and GDP.
There is still work to do. Infrastructure must keep up. Fraud controls must tighten. Regulations need to protect users without killing innovation. But the last 12–18 months of data tell a consistent story: Nigeria is moving steadily toward a cash-light economy, and real-time payments are at the centre of that shift.

Payments System Policy
Home
Payments System Policy
PSV2025
Payments System Vision 2025
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) launched and officially presented to the public the Payments System Vision 2025 (PSV 2025) on November 24, 2022. The Vision provides a five-year strategic roadmap for the Nigeria payments system to strengthen adoption of electronic payment, enhance safety, reliability and resilience of the system, account for new products and participants, foster financial inclusion and catalyse Nigeria's economic growth and development.
The emerging payments initiatives and schemes identified to achieve the above objectives are captured in the PSV 2025 with 10 (ten) key recommendations highlighted below to further facilitate the following objectives:
The CBN will review the core payments infrastructure and switching platform to ensure continued capability to meet payments demand. The potentials for Request for Payment (RfP) schemes will also be reviewed and the deployment of contactless solutions, contactless cards, and quick response code etc will be facilitated.
Create Open Banking roadmap for Nigeria, define a library of APIs supported by local market and consider the implementation of a regulatory sandbox that is appropriate for the Nigerian market.
Drive Agent Banking initiative and support the industry to explore solution that aid financial inclusion to accelerate the availability of basic banking and financial services to the unbanked.
Explore Blockchain solution such as Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) for the Naira, monitor the deployment of Blockchain solutions and the potentials for 'Smart Contract' solutions in other countries to develop strategy for their possible adoption in Nigeria.
Develop a regulatory framework for potential implementation of 'Stable Coins', and work with Securities & Exchange Commission to jointly develop regulatory framework for Initial Coin Offerings (ICO) in the event of the adoption of ICO-based investment solution in Nigeria.
Identify use cases for Big Data that has potential access to data in the payments system as well as support economic analysis.
Review the minimum-security requirements for banks to ensure they reflect the current industry best practices. The payments system architecture will also be reviewed to ensure that the minimum standards for user authentication are included as part of a multi-layer security solution.
Continue to support the use of Bank Verification Number (BVN) as an effective tool to check fraud in addition to exploring more potential use of BVN.
Request banks to strengthen consumer protection by issuing minimum required standards for swifter dispute resolution in Nigeria.
Interoperability shall continue to be a core principle of payments system in Nigeria. The tests to ensure compliance and license renewal, shall continue to form part of periodic assessment of Payments Service Providers.
OVERSIGHT
In its effort to strengthen the oversight of the payments system, the Bank established the Oversight and Compliance Division (OCD) in the Payments System Management Department for effective monitoring of existing and planned payments system.
The OCD activities include but are not limited to monitoring and oversight functions (onsite and offsite) on the payments system in Nigeria with particular reference to functions of Card and Payment Schemes (Schemes) Switching and Processing Companies (Switches), Mobile Money Operators (MMOs), Payment Terminals Service Providers (PTSPs), Payments Solution Service Providers (PSSPs), Payment Terminal Service Aggregators (PTSAs) and other Payment Service Providers.
In this regard, the Bank has issued various licences to Payment Service Providers for operation in the Nigerian payments system.

Follow the Money
Here is why bank transfers in Nigeria will cost more from 2026
By
Temitayo Jaiyeola
22nd Dec, 2025
Get TC updates in your Newsfeed
Image source: ITWeb
Share
Share
This is Follow the Money , our weekly series that unpacks the earnings, business, and scaling strategies of African fintechs and financial institutions. A new edition drops every Monday.
From January 2026, sending ₦50,000 ($34.14) through your bank app could cost you ₦100 in transfer fees. Not because banks suddenly changed their pricing, but because the Nigerian government has changed who pays for electronic transfers.
Five years after replacing stamp duty with the Electronic Money Transfer Levy (EMTL), Nigeria is reintroducing stamp duties , according to new budget documents , and the shift will change how everyday transfers work. Introduced in 2020 , EMTL imposed a flat, one-off ₦50 charge on electronic transfers of ₦10,000 ($6.83) and above, paid by the receiver, as part of the government’s push to diversify revenue away from oil and tap into Nigeria’s booming e-payments market, which hit ₦1 quadrillion in 2024.
However, under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025 , EMTL has been renamed stamp duty and expanded to include duties payable on chargeable instruments, including tax stamps, electronic tagging, electronic receipts, and certificate issuance.
“Compliance with the approved Regulations governing the administration of Stamp Duties will be enforced to ensure full collections over the medium term,” the Nigerian government wrote in a budget document.
For transfers, the ₦50 charge will no longer be a one-off deduction on funds received. From 2026, the obligation shifts to the sender, turning stamp duty into an additional cost layered on top of existing transfer fees.
While the shift from EMTL to stamp duty rewrites who bears the cost of digital payments, it also makes what was once an invisible deduction on money received become a visible, repeated expense on every transfer sent, reshaping consumer behaviour, fintech pricing models, and the government’s long-term bet on electronic payments as a dependable revenue stream.
How it affects transfers
Today, most bank customers already pay transfer fees : ₦10 for transfers below ₦5,000; ₦25 for transfers between ₦5,001 and ₦50,000; ₦50 for transfers above ₦50,000.
From 2026, sending ₦10,000 or more will cost between ₦75 and ₦100 per transfer, depending on the amount. While the money received stays whole, the sender pays more in transfer fees.

The Impact:
The ₦50 levy is no longer deducted from the receiver. You (the sender) must pay it on top. This adds ₦ 0 to your costs every year.
Source: Nigeria Tax Act 2025 / Current Banking Tiers • Built by TechCabal
For businesses, this technically removes the need to pass on an extra ₦50 deduction to customers receiving payments. For PoS agents, who often bake every possible charge into withdrawal fees, it eliminates the extra ₦50 deduction on transfers above ₦10,000. This increases the transfer burden for transaction initiators, unlike before, when it was split between both the receiver and sender.
For fintechs like OPay and PalmPay , which built growth on cheap or outright free transfers, transactions above ₦10,000 will now come at an extra cost to senders. Digital payments in Nigeria grew because they were fast, simple, and relatively affordable. Each new layer of fees chips away at that advantage. While stamp duty will help fund the growing needs of governance, Nigerians will pay for it, ₦50 at a time, every time they send money, across all platforms.
The numbers
EMTL is a small but growing source of government revenue. It generated ₦219.11 billion ($149.61 million) in 2024, beating its ₦174.24 billion ($118.98 million) projection. Between January and July 2025 alone, it had already earned ₦211.75 billion ($144.59 million), over 92% of its ₦228.85 billion ($156.27 million) full-year target.
That growth was driven largely by the extension of the levy to fintech platforms such as OPay, PalmPay, and Moniepoint. Initially, EMTL applied only to banks. Since December 2024 , fintech transactions have been brought fully into the net
With the expanded stamp duty regime, the government is projecting ₦456.07 billion ($311.42 million) in revenue in 2026, rising to ₦579.82 billion ($395.92 million) in 2027 and ₦752.45 billion ($513.79 million) in 2028. These figures are already baked into medium-term budget planning, making stamp duty a key pillar of fiscal certainty.
Also, under EMTL, revenue was shared between the federal government (15%), state governments (50%), and local governments (35%). Under the new tax law, the federal share drops to 10%, while states take 55%.
Replacing EMTL with stamp duty is part of a broader package of tax reforms set to take effect in January 2026. “The new tax laws were enacted to improve tax collection and grow non-oil revenue,” the government said in a new budget document .
The extra ₦50 people have to pay is insignificant in isolation, but multiplied across millions of daily transfers, it adds up to hundreds of billions for the government, and steadily erodes affordability for Nigerians who rely on digital payments to move money quickly and cheaply.

By
ThePoint -
October 13, 2026 0
374

Nigeria’s interest payments rose to N7.7 trillion in the first half of 2026, from N5.6 trillion in the corresponding period of 2025, amid high domestic borrowing costs, according to the World Bank.
The interest payment gulped 124.19 percent of the federal government revenue.
In its 2026 Nigeria Development Update (NDU) titled ‘Beyond the Federal Purse: How Higher Revenues Reshaped State Priorities,’ the bank said interest payments increased to 3.1 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) from 2.5 percent a year earlier.
According to the report, the increase came as federal government revenue improved to N6.2 trillion (2.5 percent of GDP) from N3.6 trillion, or 1.6 percent of GDP, in the first half of 2025.
“Federal revenues rose to about 2.5 percent of GDP (N6.2 trillion), from 1.6 percent of GDP (N3.6 trillion) a year earlier, supported by a recovery in oil receipts, stronger corporate tax collections, and higher independent revenues, while customs revenues held stable and VAT collections stayed comparatively flat,” World Bank said.
“Interest payments increased to 3.1 percent of GDP (N 7.7 trillion) from 2.5 percent (N5.6 trillion) amid high domestic borrowing costs. Reported capital spending fell to 0.3 percent of GDP (N0.7 trillion) from 1.0 percent while other expenditure remained at 1.3 percent.”
The bank said total expenditure declined slightly to N16.1 trillion, or 6.5 percent of GDP, from N14.6 trillion (6.6 percent of GDP), in the corresponding period of 2025.
However, the bank said the composition of spending shifted, with personnel costs rising to N4.2 trillion from N3.7 trillion following wage adjustments, although spending remained unchanged at 1.7 percent of GDP.

Home / Business / Receiving money from abroad in Nigeria: What CBN’s 2026 remittance rules change
Receiving money from abroad in Nigeria: What CBN’s 2026 remittance rules change
By : Priscilla Iwedike
Date:
23 October 2026 9:40pm WAT
Share :
Follow Us on Google Discover
Since 1 May 2026, licensed money transfer operators such as Western Union and MoneyGram have had to route every remittance they deliver in Nigeria through naira settlement accounts at Nigerian banks, under a Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) circular dated 24 March 2026. The change comes as more money arrives through those operators. In a statement on 30 August 2026, the CBN said inflows through them reached $947 million in July, a record for a single month. They totalled $3.8 billion in the first seven months of the year, 50.2 per cent more than in the same period of 2025. The CBN governor, Olayemi Cardoso, has set a target of $1 billion a month. Two years earlier, the bank had reported $553 million for July 2024 as an all-time high.
Remittances as a whole are much larger. Money sent home by Nigerians living abroad is one of the country’s largest sources of foreign exchange. World Bank data, last updated in October 2026, put personal remittances received by Nigeria at an estimated $22.8 billion in 2025, up from $19.5 billion in 2023. In 2024, Nigeria received $22.1 billion, about 39 per cent of the $57.2 billion recorded for the whole of sub-Saharan Africa and roughly three times the amount received by Ethiopia, the next largest recipient in the region.
For the families and businesses at the receiving end, a common problem is a transfer that the sender says has left but that has not yet arrived.
Did the CBN ban dollar payouts?
Leadership newspaper reported the March circular as a ban on foreign currency payouts from 1 May. The circular itself, reference TED/FEM/FPC/PUB/001/002 and signed by Musa Nakorji, director of the CBN’s Trade and Exchange Department, deals with settlement accounts and pricing and does not mention the currency in which recipients are paid. The requirement that licensed operators pay recipients in naira dates from the CBN’s revised guidelines of 31 January 2024, as the law firm Udo Udoma & Belo-Osagie notes in its analysis of the circular.
Advertisement
The operator rules do not cover money sent directly from a bank abroad to a Nigerian bank over Swift. A payment of that kind in foreign currency can be credited to a domiciliary account.
Two routes into a Nigerian account
Money from abroad usually reaches Nigeria by one of two routes.
The first is a bank transfer. The sender’s bank sends a payment instruction over Swift, the messaging network that banks use for international payments, while the money itself moves through accounts that banks hold with each other. Nigerian banks keep foreign currency accounts with correspondent banks abroad, and the payment travels to that account, sometimes through one or more intermediary banks, before the Nigerian bank credits its customer. A payment sent in dollars or another foreign currency can be credited to a domiciliary account, the foreign currency account that Nigerian banks offer alongside naira accounts.
The second route is a licensed international money transfer operator (IMTO), such as Western Union or one of the app-based services. The sender pays the operator abroad, and the operator settles with a partner bank in Nigeria, which pays the recipient.
Advertisement
The two routes are governed by different rules, and the rules for the second have changed several times since 2020.
Rule changes since 2020
On 30 November 2020, the CBN directed that recipients of remittances sent through IMTOs should receive the money in foreign currency, either as dollar cash or as a credit to a domiciliary account at a bank of their choice. A clarification dated 2 December 2020 required operators to pay the funds into the correspondent accounts of their agent banks, which would then pay the recipients. A separate circular of 30 November 2020 allowed holders of ordinary domiciliary accounts funded by electronic or wire transfer to use the money without restriction for eligible transactions, while cash deposits stayed under the existing rules.
In March 2021, the CBN introduced the “Naira 4 Dollar” scheme, which paid recipients N5 for every dollar received through licensed operators. It was first set to run for two months, was extended in May 2021 and ended on 30 June 2023, the same month the CBN merged the segments of the official foreign exchange market into the Investors’ and Exporters’ window.
In July 2023, the CBN restored the option of receiving remittances in naira, priced at the rate of that window on the day of the transaction. In September 2023, it required operators to quote rates within 2.5 per cent either side of the previous day’s closing rate.
Both measures were replaced on 31 January 2024. The CBN’s revised guidelines for international money transfer services limit licensed operators to inbound transfers and require them to pay recipients in naira only, through a bank account or in cash, with no cash payments above $200. Operators must use the prevailing rate in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market on the day the transfer is received. A circular issued the same day removed the 2.5 per cent band. The guidelines also set a minimum share capital of $1 million and a licence application fee of N10 million.
The latest change is the circular of 24 March 2026, “Measures to Further Deepen Diaspora Remittances and Compliance”, which took effect on 1 May 2026. It requires every licensed operator to open naira settlement accounts with authorised dealer banks and to route all its transactions through them, including payments to recipients. Banks may transfer foreign currency from those accounts to other banks and to approved market participants, including licensed bureaux de change. Operators must use real-time prices from Bloomberg BMATCH as a guide when they price transactions.
Remittances to Nigeria in figures
In the World Bank’s series, recorded inflows rose from $1.4 billion in 2000 to $18.0 billion in 2007. Since then they have stayed between about $17 billion and $24 billion a year, with a high of $24.3 billion in 2018 and a low of $17.2 billion in 2020. The series puts the 2016 total at $19.7 billion. For 2026, balance of payments figures published by the CBN put personal transfers, which include workers’ remittances, at $11.1 billion in the first half of the year.
Measured against the size of the economy, the change has been larger. Remittances were equal to 8.8 per cent of gross domestic product in 2024, up from 4.0 per cent in 2023. Most of that rise reflects the smaller dollar value of the economy, which the World Bank puts at $252 billion in 2024, down from $487 billion a year earlier.
The number of Nigerians living abroad has also grown. United Nations estimates count about 2.1 million international migrants born in Nigeria in mid-2024, up from about 394,000 in 1990.
Where a transfer can slow down
The cross-border leg is usually quick. Swift says its data show three in four cross-border payments arriving at the recipient’s bank within ten minutes. The longer wait usually comes at the end: Swift estimates that the final domestic step, from the receiving bank to the customer’s account, can take around 80 per cent of the total processing time.
Advertisement
A receiving bank may hold a payment while it reviews it under anti-money laundering rules, or while it resolves beneficiary details that do not match its records, for example a misspelt name or an account number with a missing digit. A payment that arrives after the bank’s cut-off time or on a non-working day is usually processed on the following business day. When a payment passes through an intermediary bank, that bank can also deduct a fee, so the amount that arrives can be smaller than the amount sent.
How a recipient can track a transfer from abroad
Each payment instruction on the Swift network includes a code of 36 characters known as the UETR, short for Unique End-to-end Transaction Reference. Intermediary banks must keep the code unchanged, so it stays with the payment from the first bank to the last. When a bank transfer is late, it is the first detail to ask for.
Senders can get the UETR from their bank, and it is often printed on the detailed payment confirmation, which banks may call the MT103 copy. An MT103 shows that the sending bank issued the payment instruction; it does not show that the money has been credited. With the UETR, the recipient’s bank can locate the incoming payment. Recipients can also check the payment themselves: a person waiting for money can track a wire transfer as the receiver by entering the UETR on an independent tracking service. One such service, uetr.ai , lets anyone check a Swift transfer free of charge. The user enters the 36-character code with the amount and date and sees the status reported for the payment, with bank codes such as ACSP (accepted, with settlement in process) and ACCC (credited to the recipient’s account) explained in plain English. Users can also ask to be emailed when the status changes.
Transfers through licensed operators work differently. They come with the operator’s own reference, such as Western Union’s money transfer control number (MTCN), and the operator’s website or app is the first place to check.
If the money has not arrived
Ask the sender for four details: the UETR or the operator’s reference number, the exact amount and currency, the date the transfer was sent, and the name of the sending bank or operator. Give them to your bank in writing and keep a copy.
The CBN asks customers to give their bank two weeks to resolve a complaint. If the bank has not resolved it by then, the complaint can be escalated to the CBN’s Consumer Protection Department, by email to [email protected] or by letter to its director, with evidence that it was first lodged with the bank.
The cost of sending money to Nigeria
The World Bank’s Remittance Prices Worldwide database tracks what money transfer providers charge. In the third quarter of 2025, sending $200 from the United States to Nigeria cost an average of 2.72 per cent of the amount. Sending £120 from the United Kingdom cost 1.96 per cent. The global average was 6.36 per cent.
Targets for cross-border payments set by the Financial Stability Board, which G20 leaders endorsed in 2021, call for three quarters of remittances in each corridor to reach the recipient within an hour by the end of 2027, and all of them within one business day. They also call for sending $200 to cost 3 per cent or less on average by 2030, with a ceiling of 5 per cent for any one corridor. On cost, both corridors to Nigeria are already under that mark.

Follow the Money
Nigeria’s fintechs built payments. Now they’re becoming banks.
By
Temitayo Jaiyeola
29th Jun, 2026
Get TC updates in your Newsfeed
Image source: Benson Ibeabuchi/Bloomberg
Share
Share
This is Follow the Money , our weekly series that unpacks the earnings, business, and scaling strategies of African fintechs, financial institutions, companies, and governments. A new edition drops every Monday.
Fintechs built their reputation by making payments faster and replacing many physical banking functions with smartphones. Now, they are becoming banks, or at least a particular kind of bank.
This year, Nigeria’s biggest fintechs have accelerated their push into banking through microfinance bank (MFB) licences as they seek to expand beyond their core businesses into full-service financial institutions.
In January, Paystack , the payments technology company now owned by The Stack Group (TSG), acquired Ladder Microfinance Bank. In April, Flutterwave, Africa’s largest payments startup, secured a national MFB licence through its acquisition of open banking startup Mono.
In May, Sycamore, a financial service group with lending and asset management businesses, told TechCabal it plans to build a deposit base of more than ₦40 billion ($29.13 million) as it expands from digital lending into banking and payments after acquiring an MFB.
An MFB licence allows fintechs to accept deposits, give loans, and earn interest income from lending, reducing their reliance on transaction fees.
But the licence does more than unlock new products. It changes the business that fintechs are expected to build. Unlike payment companies, which earn money every time customers move money, banks earn by keeping deposits, lending them out and managing the risks that come with that business.
Yet a microfinance bank is not a commercial bank. It is a specialised banking institution with a narrower mission to mobilise deposits, lend primarily to households and small businesses, and operate within strict prudential limits set by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN).
Deposits change the economics
Payment businesses make money when customers move money. Banks make money when customers leave money behind.
Deposits become a permanent funding base. Fintechs can earn a transfer fee on customer accounts. At least ₦10 on transfers between ₦5,000 and ₦50,000, and ₦50 on those above ₦50,000, and interest income on loans.
The Revenue Engine: Payments vs. Lending
Transfer fees are strictly regulated, but when combined with a deposit base, the economics of a fintech change completely.

Top 20 Nigerian Fintech Companies in 2026
The top fintech companies in Nigeria shaping digital banking and payments.
Follow Condia on Google News
Explainer By Daxonétété William
August 7, 2026 13 minute read
Nigeria’s fintech industry is the most funded sector in the country’s startup ecosystem. When it comes to sending money to relatives, making online payments, financial savings, getting a loan, or investing, fintechs have become reliable channels.
So, which companies matter most? In this article, we look at some of the top Nigerian fintech companies by market reach, products, transaction volume, funding, infrastructure, and overall influence.
But before we dive into the top 20 Nigerian fintechs to watch in 2026, it’s important to understand what fintech means in Nigeria and why the sector is experiencing such rapid growth.
What Are Fintech Companies in Nigeria? How the Fintech Industry Evolved
In Nigeria, fintech is simply technology that makes financial services better, faster, and simpler for millions of citizens. It covers software, mobile apps, APIs, and payment systems that are now part of daily life across the country.

Read Story
Nigeria’s fintech industry didn’t start as an independent sector. In the beginning, Nigerian fintech companies built solutions on top of existing banking infrastructure, improving user experience and convenience for local customers. But banks still handled the actual movement of money. They controlled customer accounts, settlement systems, and regulatory relationships.
That changed when a new generation of startups began building their own payment infrastructure. Interswitch was one of the earliest examples. Founded in 2002, it helped build Nigeria’s electronic payment system at a time when cash and physical banking still dominated.
By the early 2010s, more Nigerian technology-driven companies emerged. These early Nigerian fintechs solved problems around payments, online commerce, and financial access for underserved communities. But they still depended heavily on partnerships with banks because the regulatory framework required many financial services to operate through licensed institutions.
In 2012, the Central Bank of Nigeria introduced the country’s first cashless policy as a pilot programme in Lagos State. The goal was to reduce cash dependence among Nigerians and encourage digital payments across the country. The policy created demand for digital payment solutions and opened doors for Nigerian fintech companies to participate more actively in the country’s financial services sector.
That October, the CBN launched the National Financial Inclusion Strategy to bring more Nigerians into the formal financial system. Until then, millions of Nigerians had no bank accounts and thus limited access to financial products. This further created an opportunity for Nigerian fintech solutions to grow and reach millions of unbanked citizens.
Between 2015 and 2020, a new group of Nigerian fintech companies emerged. Earlier companies like Paga had already made digital banking easier for Nigerian consumers, while fintechs like Paystack and Flutterwave focused on helping Nigerian businesses accept and manage online payments.
In 2018, the Central Bank of Nigeria introduced the Payment Service Bank framework. This allowed approved non-bank institutions to provide banking services, especially to underserved Nigerians in rural and semi-urban areas.
These policy changes transformed fintech regulation in Nigeria. Fintech companies were no longer just technology providers. They were becoming independent players who could build payment platforms, wallets, switching systems, and lending products under regulatory oversight. Today, many of the top Nigerian fintechs operate under this framework.
Why Fintech Companies Are Growing in Nigeria
Several factors like local market demand, the push for financial inclusion, rapid technology adoption, and the everyday need for easier money movement across the country drive fintech growth in Nigeria.
As financial transactions become unavoidable, every adult Nigerian sends and receives money, pays for goods, or manages business transactions. This makes fintech a mass-market product in Nigeria.
Solving Old Banking Problems (People Wanted Something Better)
Before fintech, you had to go to a Nigerian bank branch, which for many Nigerians meant long queues and lots of paperwork. It wasted time they could have used for work or business.
This frustration made many Nigerians look for a faster way. Fintech gave them that option, and today, Nigerian fintech apps are the primary banking tool for millions. With just a smartphone, any Nigerian could send or receive money in minutes no matter their reading level or location. Mobile apps, digital wallets, and local agents made payments easy. Once Nigerians saw how convenient it was, they quickly switched from traditional banks to fintech apps. This growing number of Nigerian users helped fintech companies expand rapidly across the country.
Making Financial Services for Everyone (Reaching More People)
Traditional banks asked for formal documents, followed strict rules, and expected customers to understand banking terms. This left out many Nigerians, especially those working in the informal sector like traders, farmers, and small business owners.
Nigerian fintech companies changed this when they built mobile apps that let Nigerian users do basic tasks in seconds, without stepping into a bank branch, and no banking knowledge needed. By serving this large group of Nigerians who had never used banks before, fintechs gained millions of new customers across the country.
Building the Tech Behind the Scenes (Helping More Fintechs Start)
Some Nigerian fintech companies do not deal with customers directly. Instead, they build the technology called APIs that lets other businesses add payment features to their own apps. This means new fintechs don’t have to build everything from scratch, which is very expensive.
Because of this, it became cheaper and easier to start a fintech company in Nigeria. More startups entered the Nigerian market, which created more competition and new ideas. The fintech boom in Nigeria also created jobs in areas like engineering, product management, marketing, cybersecurity, and compliance.
How Fintech Companies Make Money in Nigeria: Investor Confidence and Funding
Nigerian fintech companies benefit from multiple revenue channels, including transaction fees, subscriptions, API infrastructure, digital lending, foreign exchange, and partnerships.
For infrastructure-focused Nigerian fintechs, revenue comes from helping other Nigerian businesses access financial systems. They may not serve millions of consumers directly, but they can earn significant revenue by powering thousands of Nigerian businesses.
With a population of over 240 million and fast-growing digital adoption, the Nigerian fintech industry has continued to grow. Nigerian fintech companies have raised some of Africa’s largest startup rounds from 2019 to date.
Paystack’s $200 million acquisition by Stripe in 2020 remains a landmark moment in the Nigerian fintech industry, and the success stories of startups like Flutterwave, Moniepoint, and LemFi continue to put Nigeria on the global map.
However, fintech in Nigeria has not only been about success stories. The Nigerian fintech sector has seen many failures too.
Okra shut down in May 2025 after raising $16.5 million. Co-founder and CEO Fara Ashiru Jituboh stepped down, and the company returned about $4 million to investors. Other startups such as Thepeer and Lazerpay have also shut down.
List of the Top 20 Fintech Companies in Nigeria
Nigeria’s fintech sector has moved beyond payments. The top Nigerian fintechs now span cross-border payments, remittances , wealth management, savings, payment infrastructure, lending, blockchain, and stablecoins.
1. Flutterwave
Category: Payment Infrastructure Founded: 2016 Founders: Olugbenga Agboola
Flutterwave, one of the top Nigerian fintechs, helps businesses accept and move money across Africa and beyond. Its products include Flutterwave for Business, Checkout APIs, Send App, and cross-border payment rails.
The company operates in more than 35 countries, holds 34 US Money Transmission Licenses, and has processed over $40 billion in transactions since inception.
In January 2026, Flutterwave bought open banking provider Mono, and in April 2026, it successfully secured a Central Bank of Nigeria microfinance license. In June 2026, Ripple invested in the company at a $3.2 billion valuation, and in July 2026, Circle Ventures also made a strategic investment.
2. Kora
Category: Payment Infrastructure Founded: 2017 Founder: Dickson Nsofor
Kora handles cross-border collection, disbursement, and multi-currency settlement for international companies operating in Africa. Its infrastructure lets businesses connect to local payment methods without building individual integrations.
3. LemFi
Category: Remittances Founded: 2021 Founders: Ridwan Olalere and Rian Cochran
LemFi is a cross-border platform for African migrants that allows users to send money internationally and deposit funds into local bank accounts.
With over 2 million global users, in January 2025, it raised $53 million in a Series B round led by Highland Europe. In May 2026, it added a $34.95 million Series B extension. Altogether, the fintech has raised $120 million since it was founded.
In June 2025, LemFi bought the UK credit fintech Pillar and currency exchange bureau Buttercrane.
4. Bamboo
Category: Wealth Management Founded: 2018 Founders: Richmond Bassey and Yanmo Omorogbe
Bamboo gives Nigerians access to US stocks through a mobile app, making international investments available to retail investors. Bamboo is a leader in the growing wealth-tech space.
5. Cowrywise
Category: Wealth Management Founded: 2017 Founders: Razaq Ahmed and Edward Popoola
Cowrywise helps Nigerians save and invest through its products, which include automated savings and access to mutual funds. Cowrywise has made structured savings and investment products accessible to everyday Nigerians.
6. Kuda Bank
Category: Digital Banking Founded: 2017 Founders: Babs Ogundeyi and Musty Mustapha
Kuda is a digital-first bank offering retail and business banking services through mobile apps. Products include transfers, overdrafts, budgeting tools, and Kuda Business.
The company has over 7 million registered users and more than 100,000 SME accounts. It has raised over $90 million, and its valuation reached $500 million in 2021.
7. Moniepoint
Category: Payment Infrastructure / Banking Founded: 2015 Founders: Tosin Eniolorunda and Felix Ike
Moniepoint has become one of the top Nigerian fintechs and one of Nigeria’s largest financial platforms, and its products include POS terminals, business banking, personal banking, and working capital loans.
The company has over 20 million monthly active users, 2 million merchants, and 10 million businesses served nationwide. It processes over $250 billion in annual payments. In 2025, it recorded ₦412 trillion ($294 billion) in transaction volume.
Moniepoint launched Moniebook in 2025 and bought the restaurant platform ORDA in March 2026. Investors include Visa, Google’s Africa Investment Fund, Development Partners International, and LeapFrog Investments.
8. OPay
Category: Digital Banking Founded: 2018 Founder: Zhou Yahui
OPay, another of the top Nigerian fintechs, runs one of Nigeria’s largest consumer finance ecosystems, with products including a mobile wallet, savings, micro-loans, transfers, bill payments, and agent services.
The company has over 50 million registered users and more than 1 million agents. Opera’s April 2026 filings value it at $3.1 billion.
9. PalmPay
Category: Digital Banking Founded: 2019 Founders: created under the Transsnet Group/Transsnet Financial umbrella, a strategic joint venture formed by Chinese smartphone giant Transsion Holdings (the manufacturer dominating Africa with Tecno, Infinix, and Itel) and Chinese internet firm NetEase.
PalmPay is a mobile-first platform for consumers and merchants with offerings including the PalmPay app, PalmPay Business, payments, rewards, and savings.
With over 35 million registered users and 1.1 million merchants and agents, PalmPay is one of Nigeria’s largest financial institutions.
10. PiggyVest
Category: Wealth Management Founded: 2016 Founders: Somto Ifezue, Odunayo Eweniyi , and Joshua Chibueze
PiggyVest helps Nigerians automate savings and investments. Major products include Safelock, Target Savings, Investify, and Flex Dollar.
The platform has over 6 million registered users. It paid out $905.9 million to users in 2025. By its 10th anniversary in April 2026, cumulative payouts crossed $2.203 billion.
11. Interswitch
Category: Payments Infrastructure Founded: 2002 Founder: Mitchell Elegbe
Interswitch is a foundational company in Nigeria’s payment ecosystem. Its products include Interswitch, Quickteller, and the Verve card scheme.
The company also runs switching infrastructure that connects banks and payment institutions. It also powers interbank switching for most Nigerian financial institutions and has been profitable for most of its existence. Visa invested $200 million in the company, and its valuation briefly exceeded $1 billion.
12. Paga
Category: Payments Infrastructure Founded: 2009 Founders: Tayo Oviosu and Jay Alabraba
Paga combines digital payments with a large physical agent network. Products include the Paga Wallet, agent POS terminals, merchant tools, and remittance infrastructure.
The company has over 20 million registered users and more than 100,000 physical agent locations.
13. Paystack
Category: Payments Infrastructure Founded: 2015 Founders: Shola Akinlade and Ezra Olubi
Paystack helps businesses accept digital payments through its products. The company serves over 300,000 businesses across Africa. Stripe acquired it in 2020 for over $200 million. In January 2026, Paystack reorganised into “The Stack Group” and bought Ladder Microfinance Bank.
14. Nomba
Category: Payment Infrastructure / Business Banking
Founded: 2016 (as Kudi.ai); rebranded to Nomba in 2022
Founders: Adeyinka “Yinka” Adewale and Pelumi Aboluwarin
Nomba is a Nigerian payment infrastructure and business banking platform providing POS terminals, online checkout, payment APIs, and business accounts.
In May 2023, Nomba raised $30 million in Pre-Series B led by Base10 Partners, with participation from Shopify. The company now serves over 600,000 Nigerian businesses and processes more than ₦3 trillion in monthly transaction volume.
Nomba’s product suite includes POS terminals, payment links, multi-currency wallets, and merchant management tools.
15. Remita
Category: Payments Infrastructure Founded: 2005 Founder: John Obaro
Remita, operated by SystemSpecs, serves individuals, businesses, and government. Its products support payments, collections, payroll, and institutional finance.
The company’s strongest role is in government finance. It runs the platform for the Federal Government’s Treasury Single Account.
16. Fincra
Category: Payment Infrastructure / Cross-Border Payments
Founded: 2021
Founders: Wole Ayodele and Gideon Orovwiroro
Fincra is a payment infrastructure company providing APIs and merchant tools for online collections, local payouts, virtual accounts, and international transactions.
Fincra obtained its commercial Payment Solution Service Provider licence from the Central Bank of Nigeria in January 2023. It secured a Canadian PSP licence in March 2026 and an Enhanced Category PSP licence from the Bank of Ghana in May 2026.
Fincra operates across more than 15 African markets and supports nine currencies. Its regulatory footprint includes Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa, Tanzania, and Canada.
17. Grey
Category: Cross-Border Payments / Remittances
Founded: 2020 (as Aboki Africa); rebranded to Grey in 2022
Founders: Idorenyin Obong and Femi Aghedo
Grey is a Nigerian cross-border payments platform that provides foreign-currency accounts, international payment collection, and global payout services. It joined Y Combinator’s Winter 2022 batch.
Grey raised a $2 million seed round in August 2022. As of June 2026, it serves close to 3 million users, supports payouts in more than 55 countries, and enables transfers to over 170 destinations.
Grey offers USD, GBP, and EUR accounts, virtual cards, and business payment tools. It is registered as an MSB with FINTRAC (Canada) and FinCEN (US).
18. Raenest
Category: Digital Banking / Cross-Border Payments
Founded: 2022
Founders: Victor Alade , Sodruldeen Mustapha, and Richard Oyome
Raenest is a Nigerian multi-currency banking platform that helps individuals and businesses receive international payments, manage foreign-currency accounts, and send money across borders.
In February 2025, Raenest raised an $11 million Series A led by QED Investors, bringing its total funding to $14.3 million. The platform now serves more than 1 million people and processes over 10,000 transactions daily.
Raenest provides USD, GBP, and EUR accounts, foreign-exchange conversion, and business payment tools. It holds an IMTO licence from the Central Bank of Nigeria and has expanded into the US, India, and the Philippines.
19. FairMoney
Category: Digital Credit / Banking Founded: 2017 Founders: Laurin Hainy, Nicolas Martin, and Matthieu Gendreau
FairMoney operates as a microfinance bank. It offers credit, retail banking, and SME loans . The company has over 10 million users in Nigeria and more than 50,000 small-business borrowers. It has raised over $55 million in funding and is one of Nigeria’s largest tech-driven lenders.
20. Cleva
Category: Cross-Border Banking / Digital Banking
Founded: 2023
Founders: Tolu Alabi and Philip Abel
Cleva is a Nigerian cross-border banking platform that provides African individuals and businesses with US dollar accounts for receiving and managing international income.
The company raised $1.5 million in pre-seed funding in January 2024, led by 1984 Ventures with participation from Y Combinator.
Cleva offers USD accounts, virtual cards, and international payment tools for freelancers, remote workers, and businesses. Cleva Payments Inc. is registered as a US Money Services Business.
These top Nigerian fintechs represent the best of what the country’s tech ecosystem has to offer. From payments to wealth management, the top Nigerian fintechs are solving real problems for millions of citizens. As the industry evolves, these top Nigerian fintechs will continue to lead the way.

Fintech Regulation in Africa, 2026: The Founder’s Guide to 10 Key Markets
Licenses, capital floors, crypto rules, and data protection duties in Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Ghana, Egypt, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Uganda, Tanzania, and Senegal. What you need, who issues it, and what changed in 2025 and 2026.
By FinHive Africa Research
Updated June 10, 2026
16 min read
NG Nigeria
KE Kenya
ZA South Africa
GH Ghana
EG Egypt
ET Ethiopia
RW Rwanda
UG Uganda
TZ Tanzania
SN Senegal
Africa’s fintech rulebook changed faster in the past 18 months than in the previous five years. Kenya and Ghana passed full virtual asset laws. Nigeria rewrote its securities act and pulled digital assets inside it. South Africa is opening its national payment system to non-banks. Ethiopia raised capital floors and forced wallet interoperability.
If you build or fund fintech on the continent, your compliance plan from 2024 is already stale. This guide gives you the current picture in 10 markets: who regulates you, which license you need, how much capital you must show, where crypto stands, and what changed in 2025 and 2026.
One rule holds everywhere. License first, launch second. Regulators across the continent now enforce perimeter rules, and several have frozen, fined, or delisted unlicensed operators.
The 10-market snapshot
Market Lead regulator(s) Core payments law Entry capital (payments / e-money) Crypto status
Nigeria CBN ; SEC (digital assets) CBN PSP Licensing Framework (2020/2021) ₦100m (PSSP) to ₦2bn (MMO, Switching) Regulated ISA 2025: digital assets are securities
Kenya CBK ; CMA (virtual assets) National Payment System Act 2011 + Regs 2014 Set by CBK per authorization category Regulated VASP Act 2025; regs rolling out in 2026
South Africa SARB ; FSCA ; Prudential Authority NPS Act 1998; reform under way Activity-based framework opening to non-banks H2 2026 Regulated 300 CASP licenses issued by end 2025
Ghana Bank of Ghana ; SEC Payment Systems & Services Act 2019 (Act 987) GHS 0 (Standard PSP) to GHS 20m (DEMI) Regulated VASP Act 2025 (Act 1154)
Egypt CBE ; FRA (non-bank) Banking Law 194/2020; Fintech Law 5/2022 Set by CBE/FRA per activity; FRA consumer-finance fintech licenses frozen Prohibited without CBE license; none issued
Ethiopia National Bank of Ethiopia NPS Proclamation 718/2011, amended 1282/2023 Birr 100m paid-up (payment instrument issuers) Prohibited for transactions
Rwanda BNR ; CMA (virtual assets) BNR Regulation 70/2024 on PSPs Set by BNR per PSP category In transition VA law drafted; CMA to license
Uganda Bank of Uganda NPS Act 2020 + Regulations 2021 UGX 100m (funds transfer) / UGX 250m+ (e-money), tiered Unregulated BoU consulting on framework
Tanzania Bank of Tanzania NPS Act 2015 + E-Money Regs 2015 TZS 2bn+ for e-money issuers; new EMI licenses limited to MNOs Restricted BoT cautions; not legal tender
Senegal BCEAO (WAEMU) 2025 Banking Law; Instruction 001-01-2024 Set by BCEAO per PI / EMI category Unregulated at WAEMU level
⟵ Swipe sideways to see the full table
Capital figures are statutory minimums at the lowest qualifying tier as of June 2026. Regulators adjust them. Confirm with the regulator before you file.
Country by country
NG Nigeria
Africa’s largest fintech market runs on a strict, category-based licensing model.
Central Bank of Nigeria
SEC Nigeria
NDPC
The Central Bank of Nigeria sorts payments licenses into four buckets: Switching and Processing, Mobile Money Operations, Payment Solution Services, and a regulatory sandbox. Pick the bucket that matches what you do. A Payment Solution Service Provider (PSSP) can run gateways and merchant collections but cannot hold customer funds. Only a Mobile Money Operator can issue wallets. Holding funds on a PSSP license is a violation that can cost you the license.
Capital floors
PSSP ₦100m · Super Agent ₦50m · MMO and Switching ₦2bn
Approval timeline
5 to 10 months across two phases (AIP, then final license)
Data protection
Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, enforced by the NDPC
Crypto
Legal as a regulated security; not legal tender
New Investments and Securities Act 2025 (signed March 2025) classifies digital assets as securities. Exchanges, custodians, and other VASPs must register with the SEC , meet fit-and-proper tests, and hold capital. Capital gains tax of up to 25% on crypto profits applies from 2026, and licensed platforms report transactions to the SEC and FIRS.
KE Kenya
East Africa’s fintech hub now has one of the continent’s most complete rulebooks.
Central Bank of Kenya
Capital Markets Authority
ODPC
The Central Bank of Kenya authorizes payment service providers and e-money issuers under the National Payment System Act and its 2014 regulations. Digital lenders fall under the Digital Credit Provider regime, which pulled hundreds of previously unregulated apps into CBK supervision and now sits within the broader non-deposit-taking credit framework. The Data Protection Act 2019 applies to every fintech handling personal data, with registration through the ODPC .
Payments
CBK authorization under NPS Act 2011; capital and governance set per category
Lending
Digital credit providers licensed by CBK; interest and disclosure rules apply
Data protection
Data Protection Act 2019; ODPC registration
Crypto
VASP Act signed October 2025; CBK and CMA split oversight
New The Virtual Asset Service Providers Act 2025 created a dual-regulator model: CBK covers stablecoins and payment-linked services, the CMA covers exchanges and investment-type services. Draft VASP Regulations 2026 finished public consultation, and providers must secure licenses before the deadlines that run through late 2026. The Finance Bill 2026 proposes annual VASP reporting to the KRA plus new digital payment taxes, including a 5% withholding tax on local card transactions.
ZA South Africa
The continent’s most institutionally mature regime is mid-rebuild, and the changes favor fintechs.
SARB
FSCA
FIC
Information Regulator
South Africa runs a Twin Peaks model: the Prudential Authority handles soundness, the FSCA handles conduct, and the SARB oversees the national payment system. Historically, non-banks needed a bank sponsor to clear and settle payments. That is ending. The SARB’s Payments Ecosystem Modernisation programme will open the national payment system to licensed non-banks in the second half of 2026, with a draft activity-based authorisation framework out for comment until June 15, 2026.
Crypto licensing
CASPs licensed under the FAIS Act since June 2023; 300 licenses approved, 14 declined out of 512 applications
AML
FIC Act registration; Travel Rule applies to crypto transfers
Data protection
POPIA, enforced by the Information Regulator
Payments reform
NPS opens to non-bank PSPs in H2 2026
New Cabinet approved the Conduct of Financial Institutions (COFI) Bill for Parliament in April 2026. It builds a single conduct framework covering open finance, payments, and crypto. Separately, draft Capital Flow Management Regulations (published April 17, 2026) replace the 1961 exchange control rules and pull crypto assets into the cross-border regime: larger transactions must route through authorized CASPs.
GH Ghana
A tiered licensing ladder lets you start small, plus a brand-new virtual asset law.
Bank of Ghana
SEC Ghana
Data Protection Commission
The Payment Systems and Services Act 2019 (Act 987) governs payments. The Bank of Ghana issues licenses in tiers, so an early-stage startup can enter at the Standard PSP level with no capital requirement and climb as it grows. Dedicated Electronic Money Issuers sit at the top of the ladder. The Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843) requires registration with the Data Protection Commission .
Capital ladder
PSP Standard GHS 0 · Medium GHS 0.8m · Enhanced GHS 2m · Scheme GHS 8m · DEMI GHS 20m
Sandbox
BoG regulatory sandbox open to innovative products, including pilots
Data protection
Data Protection Act 2012 (Act 843)
Crypto
Legal and licensed under the VASP Act 2025 (Act 1154)
New Parliament passed the Virtual Asset Service Providers Act, 2025 (Act 1154) on December 19, 2025. The Bank of Ghana is the primary licensing authority through a new Virtual Assets Regulatory Office , working with the SEC and the Financial Intelligence Centre. All VASPs serving Ghana residents had to register with the central bank by March 5, 2026, and licensing rolls out in phases through 2026 with FATF-aligned AML and Travel Rule duties.
EG Egypt
Two regulators split the market, and one of them just hit pause on new entrants.
Central Bank of Egypt
Financial Regulatory Authority
Egypt divides fintech by perimeter. The Central Bank of Egypt regulates banking, payments, wallets, and aggregators under Banking Law 194 of 2020. The Financial Regulatory Authority regulates non-bank financial services, including consumer finance, microfinance, leasing, and factoring, under Fintech Law 5 of 2022. Each side runs its own sandbox: the CBE’s banking sandbox (since 2019) and the FRA’s CORBEH sandbox. The Personal Data Protection Law 151 of 2020 applies across both.
Banking-side
CBE licenses payments, wallets, and digital banks under Law 194/2020
Non-bank side
FRA licenses fintech-enabled NBFS under Law 5/2022
Data protection
PDPL 151/2020
Crypto
Prohibited without a CBE license; no licenses issued to date
New The FRA suspended new establishment licenses for consumer finance fintechs for one year, renewable at its discretion, after 182% sector growth. Incumbents gain a moat; new entrants must wait or partner. The FRA also plans phased Basel III capital standards for non-bank financial institutions and a unified consumer credit database in 2026.
ET Ethiopia
A newly opened market with strict new rules and a 100 million birr entry ticket.
National Bank of Ethiopia
Ethiopia opened payments to foreign investors through the National Payment System (Amendment) Proclamation 1282/2023, and the sector is moving fast. The National Bank of Ethiopia licenses payment instrument issuers and payment system operators. Directive ONPS/10/2025, effective May 12, 2025, rewrote the rules: higher capital, mandatory wallet-to-wallet interoperability through the national switch, and required integration with the Ethiopian Instant Payment System (EIPS). Crypto transactions remain banned.
Capital floor
Birr 100m paid-up, in cash, with a local bank; existing holders must comply by June 2027
Transaction limits
Level 2 wallets: Birr 300k daily, Birr 150k max balance, Birr 75k P2P cap
Security
Two-factor authentication above Birr 5,000; security audits every 6 months
Data protection
Personal Data Protection Proclamation 1321/2024
New Directive ONPS/10/2025 also caps single-person ownership at 60% of a payment issuer and limits non-bank, non-telecom entities to 40% of shares. CEOs need 7 years of executive experience. Foreign banks can now enter under Directive SBB/94/2025. Plan for governance and localization costs, not just capital.
RW Rwanda
A small market with big regulatory ambition and a fast, structured licensing path.
National Bank of Rwanda
Capital Market Authority
NCSA
The National Bank of Rwanda (BNR) licenses payment service providers under Regulation 70/2024, which forced all existing PSPs to recategorize their licenses by September 18, 2024 or face revocation. The BNR runs an active regulatory sandbox and has licensed regional players such as Pesapal. Rwanda’s Law 058/2021 on personal data protection applies, supervised by the National Cyber Security Authority. The national fintech strategy targets Kigali as a regional financial hub.
Payments
BNR licensing under Regulation 70/2024; categories cover PSPs, e-money issuers, operators
Sandbox
BNR regulatory sandbox open to local and foreign fintechs
Data protection
Law 058/2021; NCSA supervision
Crypto
Draft law shifts Rwanda from restriction to regulation
New Rwanda drafted a law regulating virtual asset business , with the Capital Market Authority set as the licensing regulator for VASPs. Regulators, the central bank, the revenue authority, and the stock exchange held joint readiness workshops in May 2026. Expect licensing to open once the law passes; position early if you run a regional exchange or custody product.
UG Uganda
Clear license categories, low entry capital, but a multi-regulator obstacle course.
Bank of Uganda
Financial Intelligence Authority
PDPO
The National Payment Systems Act 2020 and its 2021 Regulations created three license types: payment system operator, payment service provider, and payment instrument issuer. You can combine categories in one application. Entry capital is among the lowest in the region. The catch is sequencing: you need NITA-U certification for your software before you file with the Bank of Uganda , registration with the Financial Intelligence Authority under the Anti-Money Laundering Act, and a registered data protection officer under the Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019.
Capital floors (lowest tiers)
UGX 100m for an e-funds transfer operator; UGX 250m for an e-money issuer
Timeline
60 days by statute; 6 months or more in practice
AML
FIA registration; keep transaction records 10 years
Crypto
Not yet regulated; BoU has published six pillars for a future framework
New Licensing momentum is real: the Bank of Uganda granted remittance fintech NALA both PSP and PSO licenses in December 2025, its third Ugandan license. The BoU has also set out six pillars for crypto regulation, signaling a structured framework ahead rather than a ban.
TZ Tanzania
A large mobile money market with one hard constraint on new wallet issuers.
Bank of Tanzania
FIU Tanzania
The Bank of Tanzania licenses payment systems under the National Payment Systems Act 2015, the Electronic Money Regulations 2015, and the Payment Systems Licensing and Approval Regulations 2015. E-money issuers need TZS 2 billion or more in paid-up capital and must hold customer funds in trust with a licensed bank. The binding constraint: a December 2020 circular restricts new electronic money licenses to licensed mobile network operators. Non-MNO fintechs enter as PSPs or partner with an MNO. The Personal Data Protection Act 2022 adds registration and compliance duties.
E-money capital
TZS 2bn+ paid-up; customer funds in trust accounts
Market access
New e-money licenses limited to MNOs since December 2020
Data protection
Personal Data Protection Act 2022
Crypto
BoT cautions against use; not legal tender
New The Fintech (Regulatory Sandbox) Regulations, GN 540 of 2024 opened for enrollment in January 2025 with quarterly intake windows. The sandbox covers digital payments, lending, AI and machine learning, and distributed ledger products. It is now the main legal route to test models the current licensing categories do not fit.
SN Senegal
One license regime for eight countries, applied one country at a time.
BCEAO
CDP (Data Protection)
Senegal sits in the West African Economic and Monetary Union, so the regional central bank, BCEAO , licenses fintechs under Instruction 001-01-2024 and the 2025 Banking Law. You need a Payment Institution license for payment services or an Electronic Money Institution license to issue wallets. The 2025 Banking Law makes prior authorization explicit: no one may present themselves as a payment institution, e-money issuer, or fintech without approval and listing on the official register. Licenses are national; operating across WAEMU means applying in each member state. Senegal’s 2008 data protection law, enforced by the CDP , applies, and AML follows WAEMU-wide rules.
License types
Payment Institution (PI) or Electronic Money Institution (EMI), issued by BCEAO
Enforcement deadline
Operators had until August 31, 2025 to secure approval
Licensed so far
PayDunya, Bictorys (PI); InTouch (EMI); Flutterwave, Mikaty (registered PSPs)
Crypto
No WAEMU framework yet; operate with caution
New BCEAO extended its licensing deadline to August 31, 2025 under industry pressure, then resumed enforcement. Over 100 fintechs operate in Senegal; only a handful hold full authorization. The gap between licensed and unlicensed operators is now the defining competitive fact in the market.
The founder’s market-entry checklist
Seven steps before you launch in any African market
The pattern repeats across all 10 countries. Run this sequence and you avoid the most common failure modes.
Map your activity to a license category first. “Payments” is not a category. Gateway, wallet issuance, switching, remittance, and lending each carry different licenses, capital, and restrictions.
Check whether you may hold customer funds. This single question separates license tiers in Nigeria, Ghana, Uganda, and Tanzania. Getting it wrong risks revocation.
Budget for capital plus time. Floors range from zero (Ghana Standard PSP) to roughly USD 1.3m equivalent (Nigeria MMO). Approval takes 2 to 10 months. Raise accordingly.
Stack the secondary registrations. Data protection registration, AML/FIU registration, and IT certification are separate processes with separate regulators in most markets. Uganda requires all three before or alongside your central bank filing.
Treat crypto as a licensed activity, not a gray zone. Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, and South Africa now license VASPs. Egypt and Ethiopia prohibit it. The era of operating unlicensed exchanges quietly is over.
Use sandboxes for anything novel. Ghana, Egypt, Rwanda, Tanzania, and Nigeria all run them. A sandbox slot buys regulatory goodwill and a defined path to a full license.
Re-check the rules every quarter. Four of the 10 markets changed core rules in the last 12 months. Subscribe to regulator circulars or a monitoring service. Stale compliance maps sink expansion plans.
What to watch through 2026
Three threads run through every market above. First, virtual asset regulation is converging on FATF standards: licensing, Travel Rule, and dual oversight between central banks and capital market authorities. Kenya, Ghana, and Nigeria set the template; Rwanda and Uganda follow next.
Second, payment systems are opening. South Africa’s non-bank access in H2 2026 is the headline, but Ethiopia’s interoperability mandate and instant payment integration push the same direction. Direct access to national rails reduces your dependence on bank sponsors and cuts settlement costs.
Third, capital floors are rising. Ethiopia multiplied its requirement to Birr 100 million. Egypt’s FRA is importing Basel III to non-banks. Expect other regulators to follow as sectors mature. Thin-capital business models face consolidation pressure.
The winners in this cycle will treat regulation as product strategy. A license is distribution: it unlocks bank partnerships, enterprise clients, and cross-border corridors that unlicensed competitors cannot touch.
